**Megan Anna Rapinoe**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-4) (born July 5, 1985) is an American former professional [soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") player who played as a [midfielder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midfielder "Midfielder") and [winger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midfielder#Winger "Midfielder"). She spent most of her career playing for [Seattle Reign FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Reign_FC "Seattle Reign FC")[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-:1-3) of the [National Women's Soccer League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Women's_Soccer_League "National Women's Soccer League") (NWSL) and the [United States national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team "United States women's national soccer team"). Winner of the [Ballon d'Or Féminin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ballon_d'Or_F%C3%A9minin "Ballon d'Or Féminin") and named [The Best FIFA Women's Player](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Best_FIFA_Women's_Player "The Best FIFA Women's Player") in 2019, Rapinoe was a member of the national teams that won the FIFA Women's World Cup in [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup") and [2019](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2019 FIFA Women's World Cup"), and the team that finished second in [2011](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2011 FIFA Women's World Cup"). She also won gold at the Olympics in [2012](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament"). Rapinoe co-captained the national team alongside [Carli Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carli_Lloyd "Carli Lloyd") and [Alex Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Morgan "Alex Morgan") from 2018 to 2020. She previously played for the [Chicago Red Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Red_Stars "Chicago Red Stars"), [Philadelphia Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Independence "Philadelphia Independence"), and [magicJack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MagicJack_(WPS) "MagicJack (WPS)") in [Women's Professional Soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Professional_Soccer "Women's Professional Soccer") (WPS), as well as [Lyon Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympique_Lyonnais_F%C3%A9minin "Olympique Lyonnais Féminin") in France's [Division 1 Féminine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Division_1_F%C3%A9minine "Division 1 Féminine").

Rapinoe's precise cross to [Abby Wambach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abby_Wambach "Abby Wambach") during the 2011 Women's World Cup quarterfinal match against [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_women's_national_football_team "Brazil women's national football team") led to an [equalizer goal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glossary_of_association_football_terms#Equaliser "Glossary of association football terms") and an eventual U.S. victory; the play received ESPN's [ESPY Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_ESPY_Awards "2011 ESPY Awards") for Best Play of the Year. During the 2012 London Olympics, Rapinoe contributed three goals and four assists to lead the U.S. to a gold medal. She is the first player, male or female, to score a [goal directly from a corner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corner_kick#Scoring_a_goal_directly_from_a_corner:_Olympico_goal "Corner kick") at the Olympic Games, having done so twice. She won both the [Golden Boot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_Golden_Boot "FIFA Women's World Cup Golden Boot") and [Golden Ball](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_Golden_Ball "FIFA Women's World Cup Golden Ball") awards at the [2019 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2019 FIFA Women's World Cup") in France.

Rapinoe is an advocate for various [LGBTQIA+](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/LGBTQIA+ "LGBTQIA+") organizations, including [GLSEN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLSEN "GLSEN") and [Athlete Ally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athlete_Ally "Athlete Ally"). In 2013, she received the Board of Directors Award from the [Los Angeles Gay and Lesbian Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles_Gay_and_Lesbian_Center "Los Angeles Gay and Lesbian Center"). Rapinoe was included in [_Time_'s 100 Most Influential People of 2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100"). In July 2022, she received the [Presidential Medal of Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Medal_of_Freedom "Presidential Medal of Freedom") from [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-5)

## Early life

Rapinoe grew up in [Redding, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redding,_California "Redding, California"), with her parents, Jim and Denise, and five siblings, including her [fraternal twin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Twin#Dizygotic_.28fraternal.29_twins "Twin")[Rachael Rapinoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rachael_Rapinoe "Rachael Rapinoe"). Rapinoe's older siblings Michael and Jenny are Denise's children from a previous marriage, while her older brother Brian is a child of Denise and Jim, as are Rapinoe and her twin. Rapinoe's father and her grandfather Jack both served in the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-sisp2019-6) As a child, Rapinoe idolized Brian and started playing soccer at age three after watching him play.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-USsoccer28jun2019-7) Brian began using drugs when Rapinoe was in second grade, and he was put in juvenile detention when he was fifteen and she was ten.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-sisp2019-6) He was subsequently in and out of various prisons including [Pelican Bay State Prison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pelican_Bay_State_Prison "Pelican Bay State Prison"). According to Rapinoe, Brian has made a determined effort to avoid drugs after witnessing her success in soccer.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-8)

## Youth career

Rapinoe spent most of her youth playing on soccer teams coached by her father.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-Carlisle-9) While attending [Foothill High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foothill_High_School_(Palo_Cedro,_California) "Foothill High School (Palo Cedro, California)"), she competed in track and basketball, and was on the [honor roll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honors_student "Honors student") every semester.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10) She played for the under-14 Northern California state Olympic Development Program (ODP) team in 1999, and for the regional ODP team in 2002.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-portlandpilots-11) From 2002 to 2005, Rapinoe, her sister Rachael, and her future national teammate [Stephanie Cox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Cox "Stephanie Cox") played for the [Elk Grove Pride](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elk_Grove_Pride "Elk Grove Pride") club team in the [Women's Premier Soccer League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Premier_Soccer_League "Women's Premier Soccer League").[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-15) Rapinoe and her family would commute 2.5 hours so she could play with the team, which is based south of [Sacramento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sacramento "Sacramento").[[d]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-18)

As a junior and senior, Rapinoe was named an All-American by [_Parade_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parade_(magazine) "Parade (magazine)") and the [National Soccer Coaches Association of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Soccer_Coaches_Association_of_America "National Soccer Coaches Association of America") (NSCAA).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] During the U.S. Youth Soccer National Championships in 2003, Rapinoe scored an [equalizer goal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equaliser_(sports) "Equaliser (sports)") in the 18th minute to tie the game 1–1 against the Peachtree City Lazers. Elk Grove finished second in the tournament after the Lazers scored a game-winning goal in the second half.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-19) Rapinoe was named to the [McDonald's](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/McDonald's "McDonald's") All-American Girls High School Soccer West Team in 2004.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-mcd2004-20)

## College career

The Rapinoe twins attended the [University of Portland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Portland "University of Portland") in [Portland, Oregon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland,_Oregon "Portland, Oregon"). They almost committed to [Santa Clara University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Clara_University "Santa Clara University") before choosing to play for the [Portland Pilots](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Portland_Pilots_women's_soccer "Portland Pilots women's soccer") on full scholarships.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-21) Rapinoe played in the [2004 FIFA U-19 Women's World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_FIFA_U-19_Women's_World_Championship "2004 FIFA U-19 Women's World Championship") in 2004, where the United States finished third.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-22)

As a freshman, Rapinoe helped the Pilots to an undefeated season and the [NCAA Division I Women's Soccer Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Women's_Soccer_Championship "NCAA Division I Women's Soccer Championship"). During the College Cup quarterfinal against [Notre Dame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Notre_Dame_Fighting_Irish "Notre Dame Fighting Irish"), she scored twice and served one assist as the Pilots won 3–1.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] During the College Cup final against [UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UCLA_Bruins "UCLA Bruins"), she contributed one goal and one assist in the Pilots' 4–0 victory.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-23) She was named NSCAA First Team All-American and was on the [Soccer America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soccer_America "Soccer America") First Team Freshman All-America. She made the [NCAA Women's Soccer Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NCAA_Division_I_Women's_Soccer_Championship "NCAA Division I Women's Soccer Championship") All Tournament Team and was the [West Coast Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_Conference "West Coast Conference") Freshman of the Year.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-24) She was also named to the All-West Coast Conference First Team and the All-West Coast Conference Freshman Team. Rapinoe started in all 25 games of the season as an attacking [midfielder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Midfielder "Midfielder"), scoring 15 goals—including seven game-winning goals—and serving 13 assists for 43 points, the fifth-highest point total for a freshman in the school's history.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-portlandpilots-11)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10)

As a sophomore in 2006, Rapinoe was among the nation's leading scorers with ten goals and two assists in eleven matches. During a match against [Washington State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_State_University "Washington State University") on October 5, she suffered a season-ending [anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) injury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anterior_cruciate_ligament_injury "Anterior cruciate ligament injury").[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-25) Despite the injury, she was one of four Portland Pilots players in history with 25 goals and 15 assists over two seasons.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10) In 2007, Rapinoe suffered her second season-ending ACL injury two games into the season.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-portlandpilots-11) She was granted a [medical hardship waiver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Redshirt_(college_sports) "Redshirt (college sports)") by the [National Collegiate Athletic Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Collegiate_Athletic_Association "National Collegiate Athletic Association") (NCAA) but did not use it.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-26) Rapinoe later said that getting injured was one of the best things that ever happened to her. She said it made her stronger and a "better person", and gave her a deeper appreciation for her endeavors as a soccer player.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-27)

After recovering from her second ACL injury, Rapinoe returned for the 2008 season and was on the starting lineup in all 22 games for the Pilots. She scored five goals and served 13 assists, helping the team to a 20–2 record.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-28) Her 13 assists ranked first for the Pilots as well as in the [West Coast Conference](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Coast_Conference "West Coast Conference") and she was named West Coast Conference Player of the Year.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-29) She was also named a [Soccer America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soccer_America "Soccer America") First-Team All-American and NSCAA Second Team All-American.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10) Although she had one more season of college eligibility remaining due to her hardship waiver, she opted to enter the [Women's Professional Soccer Draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_WPS_Draft "2009 WPS Draft") instead.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-30) Rapinoe's 88-point career, including 30 goals and 28 assists over 60 games, ranks tenth in the school's history.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10)

## Club career

### 2009–2011: Women's Professional Soccer

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Megantheearlyyears.jpg/250px-Megantheearlyyears.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Megantheearlyyears.jpg)

Rapinoe during the 2009 WPS All-Star Game

Rapinoe was selected second overall in the [2009 WPS Draft](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_WPS_Draft "2009 WPS Draft") by the [Chicago Red Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Red_Stars "Chicago Red Stars") for the [inaugural season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Women's_Professional_Soccer_season "2009 Women's Professional Soccer season") of [Women's Professional Soccer (WPS)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Women's_Professional_Soccer "Women's Professional Soccer"), the highest division of soccer in the United States at the time.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-31) She scored two goals and assisted on three others during her debut season for the Red Stars.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-sw_stats-32) In August 2009, she was named to the league's All-Star Team[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-33) and played in the [2009 WPS All-Star Game](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_WPS_All-Star_Game "2009 WPS All-Star Game") against the Swedish team [Umeå](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ume%C3%A5_IK "Umeå IK"), who were champions of the [Damallsvenskan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damallsvenskan "Damallsvenskan") league.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-34) In 2010, Rapinoe appeared in 20 games and scored one goal.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10)

In December 2010, Rapinoe signed with the expansion team [Philadelphia Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Independence "Philadelphia Independence") after the Red Stars ceased operations.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-35) She appeared in four games and scored one goal before being traded to [MagicJack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MagicJack_(WPS) "MagicJack (WPS)") while she was in Germany for the [2011 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup match against the [Boston Breakers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Breakers "Boston Breakers") on August 17, 2011, Rapinoe scored a goal during the team's 3–1 win.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-44) MagicJack was defeated 2–0 by the [Philadelphia Independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philadelphia_Independence "Philadelphia Independence") in the final.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-45)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-46) On October 25, the WPS voted to terminate the MagicJack franchise, leaving Rapinoe a free agent for the 2012 season.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-47) The league suspended operations in early 2012.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-48)

FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_FC_(W-League) "Sydney FC (W-League)") as a guest player for two games.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-49) In her second game season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011-12_W-League "2011-12 W-League").[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-50)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-51) During the summer of 2012, Rapinoe and fellow national team members [Hope Solo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Solo "Hope Solo"), [Sydney Leroux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Leroux "Sydney Leroux"), [Alex Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Morgan "Alex Morgan") and [Stephanie Cox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Cox "Stephanie Cox") played on a limited basis with the [Seattle Sounders Women](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Sounders_Women "Seattle Sounders Women") between commitments with the national team as they prepared for the [2012 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_Summer_Olympics "2012 Summer Olympics").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-52) Sounders head coach [Michelle game."[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-53) Rapinoe made two appearances during the regular season with the team, serving two team,[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-55)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-56) the Sounders sold out nine of their ten home matches at the 4,500-capacity [Starfire Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Starfire_Stadium "Starfire Stadium").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ssw_attendance-57) The average ### 2013–2014: Lyon

[![Image 11](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/13/20130929_-_PSG-Lyon_040.jpg/250px-20130929_-_PSG-Lyon_040.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:20130929_-_PSG-Lyon_040.jpg)

Rapinoe with [Olympique Lyonnais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OL_Lyonnes "OL Lyonnes") in 2013

In January 2013, Rapinoe signed for six months with [Olympique Lyonnais](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OL_Lyonnes "OL Lyonnes"), the French club that had previously won six consecutive French league championships and two straight European titles. Rapinoe's monthly salary was reportedly €11,000, (roughly $14,000).[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-nytimes_20130410-58) Rapinoe played in six regular-season matches for the team, scoring two goals. She played primarily as a [left winger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winger_(sports) "Winger (sports)") in the squad's [4–3–3 formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Formation_(association_football)#4%E2%80%933%E2%80%933 "Formation (association football)").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-sw_stats-32)

Rapinoe made her [UEFA Women's Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UEFA_Women's_Champions_League "UEFA Women's Champions League") debut during the [2012–13 quarterfinal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012-13_UEFA_Women's_Champions_League "2012-13 UEFA Women's Champions League") against [Malmö](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FC_Roseng%C3%A5rd "FC Rosengård") on March 20, scoring one goal in Lyon's 5–0 victory.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-uefa_bio-59)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-60) She later scored a goal and served an assist in a 6–1 win over [Juvisy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FCF_Juvisy "FCF Juvisy") in the semifinal.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-61) Lyon was defeated by [VfL Wolfsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/VfL_Wolfsburg "VfL Wolfsburg") 1–0 in the final.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-uefa_bio-59) During the 2013–14 season,[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-62) Rapinoe scored three goals in her eight appearances for the club.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-sw_stats-32) During the [2013–14 Champions League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013-14_UEFA_Women's_Champions_League "2013-14 UEFA Women's Champions League"), she made four appearances for Lyon and scored one goal.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-UEFACL_2013_bio-63)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-64) In June 2013, Rapinoe left Lyon earlier than planned to play for [Seattle Reign FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Reign_FC "Seattle Reign FC"). During her time with Lyon, Rapinoe scored eight goals in 28 matches across all competitions.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-:3-65)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-66)

### 2013–2023: Seattle Reign

[![Image 12: [icon]](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1c/Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg/20px-Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wiki_letter_w_cropped.svg)This section **needs expansion**. You can help by [making an edit request](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Talk%3AMegan_Rapinoe&preload=Template%3ASubmit+an+edit+request%2Fpreload&action=edit&section=new&editintro=Template%3AEdit+fully-protected%2Feditintro&preloadtitle=Protected+edit+request+on+19+September+2026&preloadparams%5B%5D=edit+fully-protected&preloadparams%5B%5D=Megan+Rapinoe)[adding missing information](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Megan_Rapinoe&action=edit&section=). _(April 2026)_

In June 2013, Rapinoe joined [Seattle Reign FC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Reign_FC "Seattle Reign FC") in the middle of [their inaugural season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Seattle_Reign_FC_season "2013 Seattle Reign FC season").[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-:1-3)[[f]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-69) Before she arrived, the team had been struggling to score goals, and had a 0–9–1 record over the last ten games.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-70) With the addition of Rapinoe and [Hope Solo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hope_Solo "Hope Solo"), as well as some other lineup changes, the Reign improved their goal-scoring ability and turned their league record around.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-71) During a 4–1 victory over the [Chicago Red Stars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Stars_FC "Chicago Stars FC"), Rapinoe scored two goals and served one assist, and was named [NWSL Player of the Week](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NWSL_Player_of_the_Week "NWSL Player of the Week") for week 16.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-72) Despite playing only 12 of the Reign's 22 [regular-season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_National_Women's_Soccer_League_season "2013 National Women's Soccer League season") games, Rapinoe was the team's leading scorer with five goals.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-73)

After suffering a foot injury during the first home match of the [2014 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_Seattle_Reign_FC_season "2014 Seattle Reign FC season") on April 14, Rapinoe sat out several games. She returned to play on July 3 against [Western New York Flash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_New_York_Flash "Western New York Flash"). Her four goals and one assist during the [season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_National_Women's_Soccer_League_season "2014 National Women's Soccer League season") helped the Reign secure the league's regular-season title, the [NWSL Shield](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NWSL_Shield "NWSL Shield"), with a 16–2–6 record.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-74) During the playoff semifinals against [Washington Spirit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Spirit "Washington Spirit"), Rapinoe scored a goal as the Reign won 2–1 and advanced to the championship final against Kansas City.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-75) The Reign lost the final 2–1, with Rapinoe scoring one goal.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-76) During the first match of the [2015 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Seattle_Reign_FC_season "2015 Seattle Reign FC season"), Rapinoe scored her first professional [hat-trick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hat-trick_(association_football) "Hat-trick (association football)") as the Reign defeated the [Western New York Flash](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_New_York_Flash "Western New York Flash") 5–1.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-77)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-78) She was named the [NWSL Player of the Week](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NWSL_Player_of_the_Week "NWSL Player of the Week") for week 1 of the season.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-79)[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-80)

In September 2019, the Reign recognized Rapinoe as a Reign Legend.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-81)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-82) During the [2021 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_National_Women's_Soccer_League_season "2021 National Women's Soccer League season"), Rapinoe co-captained the team with [Lauren Barnes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lauren_Barnes "Lauren Barnes") and scored six goals in 12 appearances.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-83)[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-84) In August 2021, Rapinoe was named [NWSL Player of the Month](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NWSL_Player_of_the_Month "NWSL Player of the Month").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-85) The Reign finished in second place during the regular season with a 13–8–3 record; they were eliminated from the [NWSL Playoffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NWSL_Playoffs "NWSL Playoffs") by the eventual champions [Washington Spirit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Spirit "Washington Spirit").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-86)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-87) On July 8, 2023, Rapinoe announced that she would retire from professional soccer after the [2023 season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_National_Women's_Soccer_League_season "2023 National Women's Soccer League season").[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-retirement-88) Her final home match with the Reign on October 6 drew a league-record attendance of 34,130, and included a ceremony honoring her.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-89)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-90)

## International career

### Youth national teams

Rapinoe played for the U.S. Under-16 team in 2002, traveling with the team to France. She played at the [U.S. Youth Soccer Association](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Youth_Soccer_Association "United States Youth Soccer Association") International Tournament in Houston in May 2003. From 2003 to 2005, Rapinoe played for the national [U-19 team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_under-20_soccer_team "United States women's national under-20 soccer team"), making 21 appearances and scoring nine goals. She played for the team Mexico in March 2003 and in the Netherlands and Germany during a European tour in July of that year. She played in three matches at the 2004 [CONCACAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CONCACAF "CONCACAF") U-19 qualifying tournament, scoring three goals. During the [2004 FIFA U-19 Women's World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_FIFA_U-19_Women's_World_Championship "2004 FIFA U-19 Women's World Championship") in Thailand, Rapinoe scored another three goals, including one against [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_women's_national_under-20_football_team "Brazil women's national under-20 football team") that secured a third-place finish for the United States.[[g]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-93)

### Senior national team

#### 2006–2009: National team debut and injury recovery

Rapinoe trained with the [U.S national team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team "United States women's national soccer team") for the first time during the team's 2006 Residency Training Camp in [Carson, California](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carson,_California "Carson, California"). She made her debut for the senior team on July 23, 2006, during a [friendly match](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exhibition_game "Exhibition game") against [Ireland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Ireland_women's_national_football_team "Republic of Ireland women's national football team"). She scored her first two goals with the team on October 1, 2006, during a friendly against [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Taipei_women's_national_football_team "Chinese Taipei women's national football team").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10) Due to two separate ACL injuries, Rapinoe did not play for the senior team in 2007 or 2008.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-94) During the group stage of the [2009 Algarve Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_Algarve_Cup "2009 Algarve Cup"), Rapinoe scored the game-winning goal in a 1–0 victory over [Norway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norway_women's_national_football_team "Norway women's national football team").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-95) The U.S. was eventually defeated by [Sweden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sweden_women's_national_football_team "Sweden women's national football team") in the final.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10)

#### 2011 FIFA Women's World Cup

At the [2010 CONCACAF Women's World Cup Qualifying Tournament](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_CONCACAF_Women's_World_Cup_Qualifying "2010 CONCACAF Women's World Cup Qualifying"), Rapinoe scored four goals and served two assists in three games.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10) After finishing third at the tournament, the U.S. defeated [Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italy_women's_national_football_team "Italy women's national football team") in a [play-off series](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_qualification_(UEFA%E2%80%93CONCACAF_play-off) "2011 FIFA Women's World Cup qualification (UEFA–CONCACAF play-off)") and earned a berth at the [2011 FIFA Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2011 FIFA Women's World Cup"). During the second play-off match, Rapinoe assisted the game-winning goal scored by [Amy Rodriguez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Rodriguez "Amy Rodriguez").[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-96) During a group stage match against [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia_women's_national_football_team "Colombia women's national football team") at the [World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2011 FIFA Women's World Cup"), Rapinoe scored to put the United States up 2–0.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-97)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-98) She celebrated her goal by picking up an on-field microphone being used for the match's television broadcast and singing [Bruce Springsteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bruce_Springsteen "Bruce Springsteen")'s "[Born in the U.S.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Born_in_the_U.S.A._(song) "Born in the U.S.A. (song)")"[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-99)

During the World Cup quarterfinal against [Brazil](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil_women's_national_football_team "Brazil women's national football team"), Rapinoe's precise cross allowed [Abby Wambach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abby_Wambach "Abby Wambach") to score an [equalizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equaliser_(sports) "Equaliser (sports)") goal in the 122nd minute of the game, setting a record for the latest goal ever scored in a World Cup match.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-100) The play later received ESPN's [ESPY Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_ESPY_Awards "2011 ESPY Awards") for Best Play of the Year.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-:4-101) With the U.S. and Brazil now tied 2–2 in the quarterfinal, the match went to a [penalty shoot-out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penalty_shoot-out_(association_football) "Penalty shoot-out (association football)"). Rapinoe scored her penalty kick as the U.S. won the shoot-out and advanced to the semifinals.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-102)[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-103) Following the match, Rapinoe was named [ESPN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ESPN "ESPN")'s Next Level Player of the Week for completing five of ten crosses while the rest of the team was 0 for 18.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-104) During the [World Cup final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup_final "2011 FIFA Women's World Cup final") against [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_women's_national_football_team "Japan women's national football team")—which was broadcast to a record-breaking international television audience—Rapinoe served her third assist of the tournament to Alex Morgan, who scored the game-opening goal.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-105)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10) The U.S. tied Japan 2–2, and were defeated 3–1 in a penalty shoot-out.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-106) After the World Cup, Rapinoe's hometown of Redding honored her with a parade and declared September 10, 2011 "Megan Rapinoe Day".[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-107)

#### 2012 London Olympics

At the [2012 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2012_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2012 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament") in London, Rapinoe scored once in her team's 3–0 group stage victory over [Colombia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colombia_women's_national_football_team "Colombia women's national football team").[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-108) She scored two goals in the semifinal as the U.S. defeated [Canada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Canada_women's_national_soccer_team "Canada women's national soccer team") 4–3. Her first goal of the semifinal was [scored directly from a corner kick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corner_kick#Scoring_a_goal_direct_from_a_corner:_Olympico_goal "Corner kick").[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-109)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-gwahl_20120806-110) She was the first player of any gender to score what is termed an "Olimpico" goal at the Olympics, and is still the only player to have accomplished it.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-111) .[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-112) Rapinoe is one of only five female players who have scored two goals during an Olympic semifinal.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-113)

The U.S. won the gold medal after defeating [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan_women's_national_football_team "Japan women's national football team") 2–1 at [Wembley Stadium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wembley_Stadium "Wembley Stadium") in front of 80,203 spectators—the largest crowd ever for a women's Olympic soccer game.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-114) Rapinoe served one assist during the final, and finished the tournament with three goals and four assists.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-115)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-ussoccer1-10) Widely regarded as one of the top players of the 2012 Olympics, Rapinoe was named to numerous "Team of the Tournament" lists including those selected by the [BBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC "BBC") and All White Kit.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-116)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-117) Rapinoe achieved a career-best eight goals and 12 assists for the national team in 2012.[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-118)

#### 2013–2014

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7d/Rapinoe_candlestick.jpg/250px-Rapinoe_candlestick.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Rapinoe_candlestick.jpg)

Rapinoe battles for the ball during a friendly match against New Zealand in 2013.

At the [2013 Algarve Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Algarve_Cup "2013 Algarve Cup") in Portugal, Rapinoe was named the Player of the Tournament, despite playing in only two of the four matches in which the U.S. competed. She was injured in practice and did not play during the final as the team defeated [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany_women's_national_football_team "Germany women's national football team") to win the tournament.[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-119) During a [friendly match](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exhibition_game "Exhibition game") against [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea_women's_national_football_team "South Korea women's national football team") on June 20, Rapinoe's corner kick ended up being the assist for Abby Wambach's 159th international goal, which set a new world record for most international goals scored by a player of any gender.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-120)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-121) During a friendly against [New Zealand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Zealand_women's_national_football_team "New Zealand women's national football team") in October, Rapinoe scored the game-opening goal on a [direct free kick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Direct_free_kick "Direct free kick") to help the U.S. win 4–1. Rapinoe was named Player of the Match.[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-122)

#### 2015 FIFA Women's World Cup

Five of the six stadiums used for the [2015 Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup") in Canada utilized [artificial turf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artificial_turf "Artificial turf"). It was the first World Cup, for men or women, to use turf instead of grass. Rapinoe criticized the use of turf, stating that grass is essential to maintain the quality and "purity" of the game.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-123)[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-124) In the United States' first group stage match against [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia_women's_national_soccer_team "Australia women's national soccer team"), Rapinoe scored twice as her team achieved a 3–1 victory.[[h]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-128) The U.S. went on to win the tournament. During training for a Victory Tour match to celebrate the World Cup win, Rapinoe tore her [ACL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anterior_cruciate_ligament "Anterior cruciate ligament").[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-129)[[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-130) Following the victory, Rapinoe and her teammates became the first women's sports team to be honored with a [ticker tape parade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ticker_tape_parade "Ticker tape parade") in New York City.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-131) Each player received a key to the city from Mayor [Bill de Blasio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_de_Blasio "Bill de Blasio").[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-132) In October, the team was honored by President [Barack Obama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barack_Obama "Barack Obama") at the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House").[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-133)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-134)

Rapinoe celebrates a goal with [Crystal Dunn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crystal_Dunn "Crystal Dunn") during the 2019 FIFA Women's World Cup semifinal against England.

Rapinoe co-captained the national team alongside [Carli Lloyd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carli_Lloyd "Carli Lloyd") and [Alex Morgan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alex_Morgan "Alex Morgan") from 2018 to 2020.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-135)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-136) The [2019 Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2019 FIFA Women's World Cup") was Rapinoe's third World Cup appearance.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-137) In a 13–0 win over [Thailand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thailand_women's_national_football_team "Thailand women's national football team") during the group stage, she scored a goal.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-138) During the knockout stage, she scored twice in a 2–1 victory over [Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spain_women's_national_football_team "Spain women's national football team"). In the quarterfinal, she scored another two goals as the U.S. defeated [France](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_women's_national_football_team "France women's national football team"). Rapinoe was named Player of the Match by FIFA for her performances in the round of 16 and the quarterfinal.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-139)

#### 2021–2023: Tokyo Olympics and 2023 FIFA Women's World Cup

On August 5, 2021, Rapinoe scored two goals—including her second career "Olimpico" goal—during a 4–3 win over Australia at the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Football_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_tournament "Football at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Women's tournament") in Tokyo, which had been postponed until 2021. The victory earned the United States the bronze medal.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-bronzemedal-149) In February 2022, the U.S. national team coach, [Vlatko Andonovski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vlatko_Andonovski "Vlatko Andonovski"), announced that Rapinoe would not be included on the roster for the [SheBelieves Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SheBelieves_Cup "SheBelieves Cup").[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-150)[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-151) On July 8, 2023, Rapinoe stated that the [2023 Women's World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2023 FIFA Women's World Cup") in Australia would be her last major tournament, and that she would retire from professional soccer at the end of the year.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-retirement-88) On August 6, the U.S. was eliminated from the tournament during the round of 16.[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-152)

## Activism

On September 4, 2016, Rapinoe [knelt during the U.S. national anthem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._national_anthem_kneeling_protests "U.S. national anthem kneeling protests") at a [NWSL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Women's_Soccer_League "National Women's Soccer League") match in solidarity with [National Football League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") player [Colin Kaepernick](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Kaepernick "Colin Kaepernick") and his protests against racial injustice in the United States.[[j]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-174) In a post-match interview, she stated: "Being a gay American, I know what it means to look at the flag and not have it protect all of your liberties. It was something small that I could do and something that I plan to keep doing in the future and hopefully spark some meaningful conversation around it."[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-175)[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-176) Later that week, managers of the [Washington Spirit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Spirit "Washington Spirit") prevented Rapinoe from carrying out her kneeling protest during a game between the Spirit and the Reign in [Washington, D.C](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington,_D.C. "Washington, D.C."). The Spirit managers, who felt Rapinoe's protests were disrespectful, played the anthem before players entered the field, so she could not "hijack" the ceremony.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-:1-177)

On September 15, Rapinoe knelt during the anthem at an international match against Thailand.[[k]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-181)[U.S. Soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Soccer_Federation "United States Soccer Federation") then issued a statement saying they expected players to stand for the anthem.[[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-182) During the [2015 World Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_FIFA_Women's_World_Cup "2015 FIFA Women's World Cup"), Rapinoe stood in silence for the national anthem.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-183) Her teammate, Hope Solo, claimed that Rapinoe almost bullied players into kneeling during the anthem, but Solo did not specify when this occurred.[[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-184)[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-185) In a 2019 interview, Rapinoe expressed displeasure with the stance of U.S. Soccer and said she would probably never sing the national anthem again.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-186)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/1b/Megan_Rapinoe_%2851131108070%29.jpg/250px-Megan_Rapinoe_%2851131108070%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Megan_Rapinoe_(51131108070).jpg)

Rapinoe speaks on equal pay at the [White House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House "White House") in March 2021.

Rapinoe has been involved in the [women's team's equal pay complaint](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._women's_national_soccer_team_pay_discrimination_claim "U.S. women's national soccer team pay discrimination claim") to the [Equal Employment Opportunity Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_Employment_Opportunity_Commission "Equal Employment Opportunity Commission") since at least 2016.[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-187) In March 2019, she, along with 27 of her [U.S. Women's soccer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_women's_national_soccer_team "United States women's national soccer team") teammates filed a lawsuit against the [United States Soccer Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Soccer_Federation "United States Soccer Federation") accusing it of gender discrimination,[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-188) hoping to achieve equal pay.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-189) In May of the following year, a judge dismissed key parts of the lawsuit, including the complaint over receiving lower pay than the U.S. men's team, but allowed other claims to move to trial.[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-190)

Rapinoe is a longtime advocate for the inclusion of [transgender women in women's sports](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Transgender_women_in_sports "Transgender women in sports"). She has characterized attempts to exclude transgender women as an effort to "legislate away people's full humanity".[[l]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-194)

## In popular culture

### Print media

Rapinoe was profiled in the July 2012 edition of _[Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out\_(magazine) "Out (magazine)")_ and in the August 6, 2012, edition of _[Sports Illustrated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports\_Illustrated "Sports Illustrated")._[[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-195)[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-196) She was featured on the cover of the March 2013 edition of _[Curve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Curve\_(magazine) "Curve (magazine)")_.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-197) The April 11, 2013, edition of _[The New York Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Times "The New York Times")_ featured an article that discussed her experience of coming out publicly before the 2012 Olympics.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-nytimes_20130410-58) In 2019, she became the first openly gay woman in the annual [_Sports Illustrated_ Swimsuit Issue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sports_Illustrated_Swimsuit_Issue "Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Issue").[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-198) She was featured on multiple covers of _Sports Illustrated_,[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-199)[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-200)_[Marie Claire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie\_Claire "Marie Claire")_,[[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-201) and _[InStyle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/InStyle "InStyle")_[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-202) the same year. In 2020, Rapinoe published an autobiography, _One Life_, which details her early life, her career highlights and setbacks, her activism for racial and gender equality and her personal relationships. The book became a [_New York Times_ best seller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_New_York_Times_Best_Seller_list "The New York Times Best Seller list") and was optioned by [Sony Pictures Television](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sony_Pictures_Television "Sony Pictures Television").[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-White-203)

## Personal life

### Relationships

Rapinoe knew she was a [lesbian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lesbian "Lesbian") by her first year in college.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-klemko-228) She publicly [came out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coming_out "Coming out") in the July 2012 edition of _[Out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Out\_(magazine) "Out (magazine)")_ magazine, stating that she had been in a relationship with Australian soccer player [Sarah Walsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Walsh "Sarah Walsh") since 2009.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-klemko-228)[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-229) After five years together, Rapinoe and Walsh ended their relationship in 2013. Rapinoe then dated the singer-songwriter [Sera Cahoone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sera_Cahoone "Sera Cahoone").[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-230) Rapinoe and Cahoone announced their engagement in August 2015.[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-231) In January 2017, Rapinoe said their wedding plans were on hold.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-232)

On July 20, 2017, Rapinoe and basketball player [Sue Bird](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sue_Bird "Sue Bird") of [Seattle Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seattle_Storm "Seattle Storm") confirmed that they had been dating since late 2016.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-233) In 2018, Bird and Rapinoe became the first same-sex couple on the cover of ESPN's _[The Body Issue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Body\_Issue "The Body Issue")_.[[222]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-234)[[223]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-235) They announced their engagement on October 30, 2020.[[224]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-236) In April 2026, Rapinoe and Bird announced they had separated after 10 years as a couple.[[225]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-237)

In a 2020 interview with [Terry Gross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Gross "Terry Gross") on _[Fresh Air](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fresh\_Air "Fresh Air")_, Rapinoe discussed the drug abuse of her older brother Brian, who had inspired her to play soccer when they were children. She explained that during his incarceration, he became involved with white supremacist groups in prison.[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-238)

### Philanthropy

Rapinoe has done philanthropic work for the [Gay, Lesbian & Straight Education Network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GLSEN "GLSEN") and the [United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Olympic_&_Paralympic_Committee "United States Olympic & Paralympic Committee").[[m]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-242) In 2013, she became an ambassador for [Athlete Ally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athlete_Ally "Athlete Ally"), a nonprofit organization that focuses on ending homophobia and transphobia in sports.[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-243) In September 2017, Rapinoe and U.S. teammate Alex Morgan were the first two women soccer players to sign on to the "Common Goal" campaign created by [Juan Mata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Mata "Juan Mata") of [Manchester United](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manchester_United_F.C. "Manchester United F.C."). As participants in the campaign, players donate one percent of their individual wages to soccer-related charities.[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-244)

### Politics

In December 2019, Rapinoe endorsed [Elizabeth Warren](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Warren "Elizabeth Warren") in the [2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_Party_presidential_primaries "2020 Democratic Party presidential primaries").[[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-245) During the opening night of the [2020 Democratic National Convention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Democratic_National_Convention "2020 Democratic National Convention"), Rapinoe hosted a panel with frontline workers of the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic_in_the_United_States "COVID-19 pandemic in the United States").[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-246) Rapinoe was one of several athletes to criticize the [U.S. Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States")'s decision to overturn [Roe v. Wade](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roe_v._Wade "Roe v. Wade") in June 2022.[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-247) She had been one of 500 former and current athletes who signed an [amicus brief](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amicus_curiae "Amicus curiae") supporting abortion rights for the [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") case in September 2021.[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-248)[[236]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Megan_Rapinoe#cite_note-249)

FROM OUR FOUNDERS

When we founded Opendorse back in 2012, student-athletes could not monetize their Name, Image and Likeness (NIL). That was
still nine years away.

As we built our company to support the biggest stars in professional sports, we did it with the understanding that every athlete –
at  every  level  –  has  a  story. They  are  supported  by  fans. They  all  make  an  impact  in  their  community.  Over  the years, we’ve  seen
the connection between student-athletes and schools at the college level as second-to-none. Still, these athletes with such close
ties  to  their  supporters  did  not yet  have  a  right  to  earn  compensation  from  brands,  sponsors,  fans,  and  donors.  But we  knew  the
day would come.

Each  generation  moved  the  ball  farther  down  the  field.  The  watershed  moment  came  on  October  6,  2020,  when  the  National
Association  of  Intercollegiate  Athletics  (NAIA)  passed  its  NIL  policy,  later  cemented  on  July  1,  2021,  when  new  state  legislation
went into effect in several states after the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) adopted its interim NIL policy. Student-
athletes  could  finally  profit  off  their  NIL.  It  happened  thanks  to  the  hard  work  of  many  trailblazers  –  athletes,  administrators,
legislators, and others – who believed, like us, that every athlete should have the right to make the most of their moment.

Opendorse began as a side-project to help one athlete – our friend and teammate Prince Amukamara – but we had moved closer
than ever to our long-term vision to Help Every Athlete.

We have learned a ton over the past decade as we’ve built industry-leading athlete marketing and endorsement solutions. When
the  new  legislation  hit,  we  were  grateful  for  our  foundation  of  knowledge  as  we  entered  the  NIL  era  of  college  sports.  Our
experience set us on a path for success as we scaled the business and took Opendorse to the next level – then each level after that.
We love constantly learning, solving problems, pushing the boundaries, and investing in our incredible team as we build something
great with people we care about. We are happy to share what we’ve learned with you.

There  are  challenges  in  the  NIL  industry,  all  of  which  come  with  great  opportunities.  There  are  ever-changing  laws  and  policies.
There  is  more  noise  and  more  distractions.  We  are  all  navigating  things  together  in  real  time,  but  our  focus  at  Opendorse  has
always remained the same: the athlete. Athletes have always, and will always, be at the center of what we do.

We’re honored to help athletes understand, build, protect, and monetize their brand. We’re proud to partner with so many schools
who  understand  the  importance  working  together  for  athlete  opportunities,  education  and  platform  safety.  We  love  how  our
platform fosters a deeper connection between fans, players, and the programs they support. We’re thrilled brands understand the
value our technology can bring them as they achieve their business goals. We are proud that Opendorse is the trusted source for
NIL data, insights, software, compliance, education, athlete deals and more.

This  project  represents  an  important  mile  marker  as  we  look  back  at  one  year  of  NIL  in  the  college  space.  Student-athletes  at
every level – from NCAA Division I to NAIA, NJCAA, and even high school in some states – are taking advantage of life-changing
opportunities.  They’re  starting  businesses.  They’re  learning  real-life  lessons  that  aren’t  taught  in  the  classroom.  They’re  making
a  greater  impact  in  their  communities  and  supporting  their  families  like  they  never  could  before.  NIL  is  ahead  of  schedule  in  the
impact it’s making for athletes across the country.

We  are  excited  to  share  the  most  in-depth  collection  of  NIL  data  and  insights  ever  compiled.  But  diving  in, we want  to  thank  the
team  members  at  Opendorse  for  the  hard  work  they’ve  put  in  to  bring  this  document  to  life.  This  project  touched  everyone  in
the company in some way, from Product to Technology, Sales and Campaigns, Operations and Marketing. We hope you enjoy this
comprehensive report detailing the first year of Name, Image and Likeness.

To see an entire industry pop up around our vision has been special, but the best is yet to come. Here’s to year two of the NIL era.
It’s going to be big!

Adi Kunalic, Co-Founder/President  Blake Lawrence, Co-Founder/CEO

took it a step further by gifting all of her teammates
with shoes during the holiday season.

EXPERIENCE

While  Division  I  stars  are  securing  flashy  deals  and  national
media coverage, NIL is making an impact for NCAA DII, DIII, and
NAIA  student-athletes.  Men’s  track  and  field  standout  Trevor
Bassitt from Ashland University has used his last year of eligibility
to  chase  another  national  championship  and  capitalize  on  NIL
opportunities.

With multiple national titles to his name and a run at the Olympic
Trials,  Trevor  Bassitt  was  debating  whether  to  turn  professional
or  use  his  remaining  NCAA  eligibility.  NIL  played  a  role  in  his
decision  to  return  for  his  final  college  season  and  pursue  his
master’s degree.

“Knowing  I  could  come  back  to  school  and  make  money  –
whether  it  is  through  endorsement  deals  or  launching  my  own
merch line, knowing that those options were available to me now
– made coming back to school to get my master’s a no brainer.”

His  status  as  a  Division  II  student-athlete  wasn’t  something
Bassitt  ever  saw  as  a  barrier.  He’s  leveraged  his  story  of  being  a
non-revenue athlete from a smaller school.

“I’ve  been  able  to  kind  of  use  it  to  my  advantage  by  making  it
part of my brand as an athlete,” he explained. “I’m an elite athlete,
but  I  often  get  overlooked  because  I’m DII  or  because  I’m  not  in
football  or  basketball.  Using  that  to  form  this  underdog  brand
that  I’m  rolling  with  here  has  been  part  of  it.  And  it’s  given  me
more  opportunities  for  the  sponsors  that  I  do  currently  have:  I
can  put  everything  I  have  into  all  of  those  sponsorship  deals  to
make sure they’re getting the best out of me and out of the deal
instead of with other athletes.”

For  Bassitt,  the  foundation  for  his  personal  brand  included
identifying what he is truly passionate about.

“Who  I  am  and  what  I  stand  for  is  actually  what  my  brand  is,”
Bassitt  said,  “because  if  I  try  to  be  something  I’m  not,  it’s  really
hard to put that stuff online. If you’re not authentic, people aren’t
going to listen to your message.”

He added that being athentic makes fulfilling deals easier.

CATEGORY PROHIBITION
Dating  back  to  the  NCAA’s  originally  proposed  legislation  from
the fall of 2020, category prohibitions were among the first places
schools  demonstrated  autonomy.  But,  it  wasn’t  until  New  Jersey
legislators  passed  the  nation’s  fifth  NIL  state  law  that  direct
prohibitions  on  categories  such  as  alcohol,  tobacco,  controlled
substances,  and  gambling  were  addressed. Though  several  states
followed  suit  with  prohibitions  on  vice  industries,  a  continuity
across  both  states  and  the  NCAA’s  subsequent  interim  policy
was that schools should set their own policies. In an environment
where there was no tested result, nor a clear frontrunner, the
process was easier for some than others.

On  June  30,  2021,  in  the  rush  to  respond  to  the  NCAA’s  interim
policy  release,  many  schools  chose  the  wait-and-see  approach.
In  less  than  24  hours,  though,  the  catch-all  Barstool  Sports  deal
made  many  act  quicker  than  they  would  have  liked.  Cited  for
noncompliance  with  policy  prohibitions  on  entities  related  to
sports  wagering,  institutions  like  Louisville  directly  advised their
student-athletes  to  steer  clear.  Similarly,  many  institutions  chose
to craft policies in tandem with their institutional values, including
Brigham Young University’s Honor Code Standards which apply to
student-athletes and non-athletes alike.

But  not  all  that  was  originally  thought  to  be  barred  was  off  the
table.  A  place  many  institutions  feared  NIL  would  bleed  into
–  the  apparel  and  pouring  rights  contracts  –  came  to  fruition
early  among  the  biggest  stars  in  sports.  Though  many  policies
have  attempted  to  caution  athletes  away  from  engaging  with
competitors, examples like Rose Zhang’s adidas contract (Stanford
is  a  Nike  school)  and  Paige  Bueckers’  Gatorade  deal  (UConn  is  a
Coca-Cola  school) were welcomed  as  the  contracts  are  limited  to
an athlete’s time outside of required team activities. Some school
policies  have  even  opened  it  up  as  far  as  to  allow  athletes  like
Florida Atlantic’s N’Kosi Perry to work with alcohol vendors.

INTELLECTUAL PROPERT Y USE
Originally prohibited under the NCAA’s first NIL proposals was the
concept of student-athletes leveraging school intellectual property
(IP) in their deals. Fear that athletes would be compensated for the
name  on  the  front  of  the  jersey  instead  of  the  name  on  the  back
led  legislators  in  Connecticut,  Oklahoma,  and  Texas  to  outright
prohibit it. (Connecticut’s law has since been amended.) Countless
schools  followed  suit  in  their  policies,  leading  to  unbranded
activations  such  as  former  Gonzaga  star  Chet  Holmgren’s  trading
card deal with Topps.

As  the  ecosystem  matured,  there  was  an  industry  shift  towards
allowing athletes to utilize school marks. This growth has allowed
athletes  to  create  engaging  content  with  a  more  organic  feel.
For  example,  Georgia  Tech  star  Kevin  Parada’s  paid  partnership
with  Invesco  QQQ,  a  corporate  sponsor  of  the  university,  meets
followers  in  a  familiar  spot  –  Russ  Chandler  Stadium. A  symbiotic
relationship between existing sponsors, the athletes, and schools,
this evolution gave way to LEARFIELD  and Opendorse’s strategic
relationship announced in April.

THE POLITICS

JUNE 27, 1984
National Collegiate Athletic Association v. Board of Regents of the University
of Oklahoma
This 7-2 decision declared that the NCAA’s control of television rights violated both
the Sherman and Clayton Antitrust Acts. It was the first Supreme Court loss for
the NCAA, and as a result, member institutions were afforded more autonomy to
negotiate broadcast rights agreements.

JANUARY 29, 2014
Kain Colter and Northwestern Football’s Effort to Unionize
Although ultimately rejected by the National Labor Relations Board (NLRB), the most
notable effort to unionize included a demand to “eliminate restrictions on legitimate
employment and players’ ability to directly benefit from commercial opportunities.”
Despite the effort falling short, the industry was put on notice for the limitations on
NIL monetization.

AUGUST 8, 2014
O’Bannon v. National Collegiate Athletic Association; Electronic Arts;
and Collegiate Licensing Company
Former UCLA Basketball player Ed O’Bannon headlined a class-action case involving
numerous individuals who claimed their rights of publicity were violated by the
inclusion of their likenesses in video games without compensation. The decision
stated that the NCAA was in violation of antitrust law by restricting payment to
student-athletes. This decision led to the NCAA changing scholarship restrictions to
allow, for the first time, institutions to provide full cost of attendance scholarships,
providing significantly more money from the institutions to most Division I
scholarship athletes.

SEPTEMBER 30, 2019
California’s Fair Pay to Play Act
The State of California became the first state to pass legislation that would prohibit
governing bodies (i.e., NCAA and Athletic Conferences) and institutions from
punishing student-athletes that accept NIL endorsement money while in college.
Despite strong lobbying against the bill, this watershed moment put pressure on
the NCAA to act on growing pressure for NIL reform. Senate Bill 206 was signed by
Governor Newsom with an effective date of July 1, 2023.

OCTOBER 29, 2019
NCAA Prepares for NIL
Less than a month after the signing of California’s Fair Pay to Play Act, the NCAA’s
Board of Governors agreed to reconsider amateurism policies across its three
divisions. Potential rule changes were to be agreed upon by January 2021 allowing
student-athletes to earn compensation for their NIL through promotions and
endorsements.

JUNE 12, 2020
Florida’s Intercollegiate Athlete Compensation and Rights Act
Florida became the third state to pass a law addressing NIL for student-athletes.
Senate Bill 646 was scheduled to go into effect on July 1, 2021, an aggressive
timeline which set the precedent for all states to follow.

THE POLITICS

OCTOBER 6, 2020
National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics Adopts NIL Policy
The National Association of Intercollegiate Athletics (NAIA) became the first
intercollegiate athletics governing body to pass legislation for NIL compensation.
The NAIA is home to 252 institutions, 21 conferences, and 77,000 student-athletes
competing in 27 sports.

JANUARY 8, 2021
Department of Justice Warns NCAA of Antitrust Concerns
The Friday before the NCAA’s highly anticipated vote on proposed NIL legislation
at the 2021 Annual Convention, the Trump administration’s assistant attorney
general of the DOJ’s antitrust division sent a letter to NCAA President Mark Emmert,
expressing concern of the NIL proposals. For fear of antitrust violation and the
weakening of their upcoming SCOTUS case, this ultimately led each of the NCAA’s
divisions to table their proposed legislation.

MARCH 2021 - JUNE 2021
Patchwork of State Laws Unfolds
Following the NCAA’s inaction at the 2021 Convention, 13 different states enacted
unique NIL legislation of their own. With nearly two dozen state laws to adhere to,
the NCAA’s ability to create consistent NIL rules grew increasingly more difficult.

JUNE 21, 2021
National Collegiate Athletic Association v. Alston
The United States Supreme Court ruled against the NCAA in a decision that stated
the organization is not exempt from antitrust regulations simply because of its
academic responsibilities. Though not directly related to NIL, Alston opened the door
for academic-related compensation for student-athletes and signaled that the NCAA
could face further legal consequences in the future. The concern became a catalyst
behind the NCAA’s ultimate decision to adopt its Interim NIL Policy.

JUNE 30, 2021
NCAA Adopts Interim NIL Policy
All three NCAA divisions adopted uniform, temporary rule changes that permit NIL
activity for its student-athletes. The association’s working policy states student-
athletes can engage in NIL activities so long as benefits are not received as pay-for-
play or improper recruiting inducements. With no federal legislation, NIL shall be
governed by state laws (if applicable) and/or individual school policies.

In  the  fall  of  2021,  fans  eagerly  made  their  return  to  college

promoting  activewear  on  Instagram.  Or  you  saw  Iowa  Men’s
basketball’s Jordan Bohannon while buying fireworks. Maybe you
ran  into  the  Virginia  Tech  offensive  line  while  eating  at  a  local
barbecue joint.

It was the first taste of NIL for most people. It was new, unknown,
and  a  little  intimidating.  But  headed  into  the  2022  fall  sports
season, like any sophomore with a year under their belt and ready
to earn a starting job, NIL is no longer a new concept. Stakeholders
in  the  game  need  to  read  the  scouting  report  of  what  could  be
coming.

It would be naïve to navigate the NIL waters in 2022 the same way
as 2021. The first year of NIL was a time of trial and error, learning,
teaching,  supporting  student-athletes,  and  for  some,  sitting  back
and observing the market.

Now it’s time to activate – for all parties involved.

Education  and  awareness  of  NIL  has  been  fast-tracked  in  the

recognized.

FROM OUR FOUNDERS

When we founded Opendorse back in 2012, student-athletes could not monetize their Name, Image and Likeness (NIL). That was
still nine years away.

As we built our company to support the biggest stars in professional sports, we did it with the understanding that every athlete –
at  every  level  –  has  a  story. They  are  supported  by  fans. They  all  make  an  impact  in  their  community.  Over  the years, we’ve  seen
the connection between student-athletes and schools at the college level as second-to-none. Still, these athletes with such close
ties  to  their  supporters  did  not yet  have  a  right  to  earn  compensation  from  brands,  sponsors,  fans,  and  donors.  But we  knew  the
day would come.

Each  generation  moved  the  ball  farther  down  the  field.  The  watershed  moment  came  on  October  6,  2020,  when  the  National
Association  of  Intercollegiate  Athletics  (NAIA)  passed  its  NIL  policy,  later  cemented  on  July  1,  2021,  when  new  state  legislation
went into effect in several states after the National Collegiate Athletic Association (NCAA) adopted its interim NIL policy. Student-
athletes  could  finally  profit  off  their  NIL.  It  happened  thanks  to  the  hard  work  of  many  trailblazers  –  athletes,  administrators,
legislators, and others – who believed, like us, that every athlete should have the right to make the most of their moment.

Opendorse began as a side-project to help one athlete – our friend and teammate Prince Amukamara – but we had moved closer
than ever to our long-term vision to Help Every Athlete.

We have learned a ton over the past decade as we’ve built industry-leading athlete marketing and endorsement solutions. When
the  new  legislation  hit,  we  were  grateful  for  our  foundation  of  knowledge  as  we  entered  the  NIL  era  of  college  sports.  Our
experience set us on a path for success as we scaled the business and took Opendorse to the next level – then each level after that.
We love constantly learning, solving problems, pushing the boundaries, and investing in our incredible team as we build something
great with people we care about. We are happy to share what we’ve learned with you.

There  are  challenges  in  the  NIL  industry,  all  of  which  come  with  great  opportunities.  There  are  ever-changing  laws  and  policies.
There  is  more  noise  and  more  distractions.  We  are  all  navigating  things  together  in  real  time,  but  our  focus  at  Opendorse  has
always remained the same: the athlete. Athletes have always, and will always, be at the center of what we do.

We’re honored to help athletes understand, build, protect, and monetize their brand. We’re proud to partner with so many schools
who  understand  the  importance  working  together  for  athlete  opportunities,  education  and  platform  safety.  We  love  how  our
platform fosters a deeper connection between fans, players, and the programs they support. We’re thrilled brands understand the
value our technology can bring them as they achieve their business goals. We are proud that Opendorse is the trusted source for
NIL data, insights, software, compliance, education, athlete deals and more.

This  project  represents  an  important  mile  marker  as  we  look  back  at  one  year  of  NIL  in  the  college  space.  Student-athletes  at
every level – from NCAA Division I to NAIA, NJCAA, and even high school in some states – are taking advantage of life-changing
opportunities.  They’re  starting  businesses.  They’re  learning  real-life  lessons  that  aren’t  taught  in  the  classroom.  They’re  making
a  greater  impact  in  their  communities  and  supporting  their  families  like  they  never  could  before.  NIL  is  ahead  of  schedule  in  the
impact it’s making for athletes across the country.

We  are  excited  to  share  the  most  in-depth  collection  of  NIL  data  and  insights  ever  compiled.  But  diving  in, we want  to  thank  the
team  members  at  Opendorse  for  the  hard  work  they’ve  put  in  to  bring  this  document  to  life.  This  project  touched  everyone  in
the company in some way, from Product to Technology, Sales and Campaigns, Operations and Marketing. We hope you enjoy this
comprehensive report detailing the first year of Name, Image and Likeness.

To see an entire industry pop up around our vision has been special, but the best is yet to come. Here’s to year two of the NIL era.
It’s going to be big!

Adi Kunalic, Co-Founder/President  Blake Lawrence, Co-Founder/CEO
