Ed Reed (Football, 1998-2001)

One of the greatest football players of all time, Ed Reed came to Miami as an All-State defensive back and kick returner. Not only did he excel at football, but he was superb at track and averaged 20 points on his high school basketball team.

![Image 23](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/08/7d880105-reed_rose_bowl-400x400.jpg)

Reed was a focal point in the 2001 National Championship game as the Hurricanes defeated the Nebraska Cornhuskers 37-14 to claim their fifth Championship. Reed recorded nine tackles.

He holds the Miami records for career interceptions (21), most career interceptions returned for touchdowns (4), most career interception return yards (389), and most single-season interception return yards (206).

Reed collected a plethora of accolades before making his way to the NFL. He was named a consensus All-American in both 2000 and 2001, a consensus All-Big East selection in 2001, and was the 2001 Big East Co-Defensive Player of the Year. He was also a named a Freshman All-American by the _Football News_ and _Sporting News_ in 1998.

Reed was drafted 24th overall in the 2002 NFL draft by the Baltimore Ravens. His career was nothing but excellent. He was a nine-time Pro Bowl selection, a five-time First Team All-Pro honoree and was the 2004 Defensive Player of the Year. He led the NFL in interceptions in 2004, 2008 and 2010 and was a part of the Baltimore Ravens’ 2012 Championship Team and finished his NFL career with 64 interceptions and 1,590 interception return yards – an NFL record.

Reed was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2019, the College Football Hall of Fame in 2018 and the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2012. He was inducted into UM’s Ring of Honor in 2017.

_– Brandon Blanco_

Varsity Four (Men's Rowing, 1988)

Miami’s championship history features a series of well-known teams and individuals that have shined on the football field, the baseball diamond, the golf course, on the tennis courts and on the track and field.

The Hurricanes also have a national championship in men’s rowing.

In 1988, the men’s Varsity 4 boat comprised of Ralph Montalvo, Fernando Mendoza, Ed Montalvo, Frank Perez and coxswain Mark Altschul won the gold medal at the Intercollegiate Rowing Association National Championship in Syracuse, New York.

The boat competed in the IRA Open Fours division and crossed the finish line in a time of 7:17:50 to secure the win.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Zack Collins (Baseball, 2014-16)

![Image 26](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/10/b93b8b36-zack_collins-400x400.jpg)

From Pembroke Pines, Zack Collins was drafted in the 27th round of the Major League Baseball First-Year Player Draft by the Cincinnati Reds.

Instead of playing for the Reds, Collins opted to enroll at the University of Miami, where he became the 2014 ACC Freshman of the Year. He was the sixth player in program history to be named _Baseball America_ National Freshman of the Year.

He ended his Hurricanes career with a career batting average of .319, started in 186 of 189 games he played in, and scored 147 runs.

He was drafted 10th overall in 2016 by the Chicago White Sox and became the first Johnny Bench Award winner in Miami history as the nation’s top catcher.

During his MLB career, Collins spent time with the Chicago White Sox, Toronto Blue Jays, Pittsburgh Pirates and Cleveland Guardians. In 2021, he caught the 20 th no-hitter in White Sox history, which was pitched by Carlos Rodon.

_– Brandon Blanco_

Bernie Kosar (Football, 1983-84)

Bernie Kosar added to Miami’s legacy as “Quarterback U” by becoming an instrumental piece for the Hurricanes. Kosar threw for 5,971 yards and 40 touchdowns in 1983 and 1984 and led Miami to its first national championship as a redshirt freshman in 1983.

![Image 29](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2021/06/0a69e25c-kosar_auburn-400x400.jpg)

In just two seasons at Miami, Kosar left his mark and still holds the school’s record for passing completion percentage.

He found a career in the NFL after being a first-round supplemental draft pick of the Cleveland Browns, where he spent nine seasons.

He ended his career with 23,301 yards and 124 touchdowns. He won a Super Bowl in 1993 as a member of the Dallas Cowboys and then ended his career with the Miami Dolphins.

It was only fitting for one of the starts of “Quarterback U” to end his football career where he made a name for himself.

Kosar was inducted into the UM Football Ring of Honor in 1999 and the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 1995.

_– Brandon Blanco_

Ray Lewis (Football, 1993-95)

![Image 30: Ray Lewis](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2017/11/120509ad-umfb101417_177-400x400.jpg)

Ray Lewis is one of the greatest defensive players to ever live. His presence was intimidating and changed the way teams got prepared to play the Hurricanes.

Lewis holds the UM single-season record for tackles with 160 in 1995. He’s also No. 2 on that single-season list with 152 tackles in 1994. He was named All BIG-EAST in 1994 and 1995 and was voted the Jack Harding MVP of the team in 1995. He opted for the NFL draft, where he made his mark as the greatest to ever do it.

The former first-round pick helped lead the Baltimore Ravens to a 34-7 win over the New York Giants in Super Bowl XXXV, where he earned MVP honors.

He was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in Canton, Ohio, in 2018, becoming the seventh Hurricane to be inducted. In 2019, Lewis was named as one of the 12 linebackers to the NFL’s 100-Year All-Time team.

Lewis was also inducted into UM’s Ring of Honor in 2017 and UM’s Sports Hall of Fame in 2006.

_– Brandon Blanco_

From Pylaia, Thessaloniki, Greece, Olga

Jack Evans (Polo, 1947-51)

For the better part of the 1980s, Miami’s football team was a force, especially when playing on its home field at the Orange Bowl.

But it turns out those teams weren’t the first Hurricanes to dominate on that venerable ground.

Between 1948 and 1951, the Hurricanes fielded a men’s polo team that competed at the Orange Bowl and won four consecutive national championships. Jack Evans was a part of those teams, serving as a captain and helping Miami post a 29-0 record during the polo team’s four years as a varsity sport.

Evans earned All-American honors twice during those four years.

Miami’s polo program was discontinued in 1951.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Orlando Gonzalez (Baseball, 1973-74)

Orlando Gonzalez came to the United States from Cuba as a 9-year-old, played baseball at Miami Senior High, Miami-Dade College and then brought his skills to Coral Gables.

![Image 36](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/09/86bb89de-orlando_gonzalez.jpg)And in his first year as a Hurricane, Gonzalez hit .338 and had 34 stolen bases. He followed that up with a senior season in which he hit .402 and stole an NCAA-record 62 bases. He helped lead the Hurricanes to their first College World Series, and though Miami finished as the national runner-up, he was selected to the CWS All-Tournament team after driving in seven runs on seven hits. Gonzalez also earned All-American honors his senior year.

He was drafted by Cleveland in 1976 and went on to play with the Philadelphia Phillies and Oakland Athletics during his four-year MLB career.

Gonzalez, who was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 1986, was the first Miami baseball player to have his number retired.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Jim Kelly (Football, 1979-82)

During Miami’s 1980s football heyday, the program earned the nickname “Quarterback U.”

![Image 39: Jim Kelly Diagnosed with Cancer](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2012/10/ff8bedac-vpbkbqeadsvkfze.20130603152633-400x400.jpg)

Jim Kelly was a big reason why.

The signal caller from Pennsylvania received a scholarship offer from his home state’s flagship program, Penn State, but opted to come to Miami where the Hurricanes wanted him to line up under center, not at linebacker.

It turned out to be an incredible move for both Kelly and the Hurricanes.

Legendary Hurricanes coach Howard Schnellenberger gave Kelly the opportunity to start as a freshman and that season, Kelly returned to Pennsylvania where he led Miami to an 26-10 upset of the Nittany Lions.

Kelly went on to throw for 5,228 yards and 33 touchdowns during his Hurricanes career. In 1980, he led Miami to a 9-3 record and its first bowl appearance since 1967, a 20-10 win over Virginia Tech in the Peach Bowl.

The quarterback was widely considered a Heisman Trophy candidate entering his senior year, but three games into the season, he was sidelined by a shoulder injury that kept him out of the game for months. He recovered in time to work out for NFL scouts in the spring and was drafted by the Buffalo Bills in the first round of the 1983 NFL Draft. Kelly, however, signed with the Houston Gamblers of the USFL.

He threw for 9,842 yards and 83 touchdowns in Houston and earned MVP honors in 1984 before the USFL folded and he joined the Bills.

In his 11 seasons with Buffalo, Kelly rewrote the Bills record book. He passed for 35,467 yards, 237 touchdowns, was a four-time Pro Bowl selection, and led the Bills to the playoffs eight times, including four straight Super Bowls.

Kelly was enshrined into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2002, the UM Ring of Honor in 2008 and the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 1992.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Mia Vallée (Women's Diving, 2019-25)

While growing up in Canada, diver Mia Vallée never imagined she’d have the opportunity to study marine biology and train in the Florida sunshine.

![Image 40](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2021/10/f7ae9a87-ee4_7522-400x400.jpg)

The University of Miami gave her the chance to do both – and win a national championship while doing it.

In 2022, Vallée became the 14 th Hurricane to win a national title under renowned coach Randy Ableman. After some tough dives in the preliminary round, Vallée posted a record-breaking score of 365.756 in the 1-meter spring finals to win the NCAA title.

Last season, Vallée capped her Hurricanes career by finishing as the national runner-up on the 1-meter – behind teammate Chiara Pellacani, who won the championship.

During her decorated Miami career, Vallée was a two-time ACC gold medalist, a three-time ACC silver medalist, and an ACC bronze medalist. She earned five All-American honors, was the 2022 ACC Diver of the Year and earned All-ACC Academic Team honors four times.

Jim Dooley (Football, 1949-51)

Jim Dooley may have spent the bulk of his football career in Chicago with the Bears as both a player and later a coach, but that career started in Miami.

![Image 43](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/09/d6c3f267-jim_dooley.jpg)A standout at Miami High, Dooley played on both sides of the ball for the Hurricanes during both his junior and senior year. He set multiple records during his college career, totaling 17 interceptions while playing with the defense and rushing for more than 1,000 yards when playing offense. In 1951, he had 10 interceptions and was named a first-team All-American by the Associated Press. He was the MVP of the 1952 Gator Bowl after hauling in a record four picks in that game.

Dooley has the distinction of being the first Hurricane ever selected in the first round of the NFL Draft, going No. 8 overall to the Bears. After an eight-year career with the Bears, he retired in 1962 and joined Chicago’s coaching staff shortly thereafter. He was eventually elevated to head coach in 1968.

Dooley was inducted into UM’s Ring of Honor in 1997 and the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 1972.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Neal Heaton (Baseball, 1979-81)

Neal Heaton played for the Hurricanes more than 40 years ago, but his name still fills the Miami record book.

![Image 46](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/09/ea901c24-neal_healton.jpg)Known as “The Heater” during his time on campus, Heaton earned multiple first-team All-American nods and remains one of the most decorated pitchers in program history. He still ranks second among all Miami hurlers with 42 career wins and third with 381 career strikeouts.

In 1980, Heaton earned 18 wins, a total no Hurricane has been able to match in a single season since, though his 16 wins a season later came the closest. In 1981, he was drafted by Cleveland, and he spent just one year in the minors before making his Big-League debut in 1982.

During his 12-year professional career that included time with Cleveland, the Minnesota Twins, the Montreal Expos, Pittsburgh Pirates, Kansas City Royals, Milwaukee Brewers and New York Yankees, Heaton posted an 80-96 record with 4.37 ERA and 699 strikeouts. He was an All-Star in 1990.

Heaton’s No. 26 is retired at Miami, and he was inducted into the College Baseball Hall of Fame in 2008. He was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 1993.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Desma Thomas Bateast (Women's Basketball, 1992-97)

A former standout at American High School in Hialeah, Desma Thomas Bateast was one of her hometown program’s impact players.

![Image 47](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/09/7690d558-desma_thomas.jpg)Bateast scored 1,284 points in her Hurricanes career and was a key contributor when Miami won back-to-back Big East titles in 1992 and 1993. Twice she was named a third-team All-Big East selection and in 1997, she earned a spot on the Big East All-Tournament team.

Her 18 made free throws against St. John’s in 1996 remain a Hurricanes single-game record and her 81 3-pointers during the 1996-97 record still rank third for a single season.

After graduating from Miami, Bateast signed with the Phoenix Mercury and played professionally in Italy, Sweden and Turkey before returning to the U.S. to play for the NWBL’s Birmingham Power.

Once her playing career ended, Bateast began coaching. She has spent time at FIU, Rhode Island, Dillard University, USF, FAU, Cleveland State and is currently an assistant coach at Florida State.

Bateast was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2012.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Dean Panaro (Men's Diving, 1991-95)

After an impressive showing that saw him place in the 1-meter, 3-meter and platform diving competitions at Junior Nationals, Dean Panaro came to Miami and unsurprisingly, found success with the Hurricanes.

![Image 50](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/09/9530d8dc-dean_panaro.jpg)Panaro – a native of Knoxville, Tennessee – won the 1991 and 1992 NCAA 1-meter diving championships. In 1993, he won both the 1-meter and 3-meter national titles.

He competed with the U.S. national team from 1989-1991 and again from 1993-1997, winning the 1-meter national championship in both 1993 and 1996. On the international stage, he posted a first-place finish in the 1991 Swedish Cup and in 1995, won the 1-meter championship at the Pan American Games, along with the 3-meter championship at the Gran Premio de Saltos event.

Panaro, who was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2004, is currently working as a voiceover talent and agent.

Horace Copeland (Football, Track & Field 1990-92)

Most Hurricanes fans know full well the impact Horace Copeland had on the football field – and rightfully so. He was a member of Miami’s 1991 national championship team and finished his Hurricanes career with 84 catches for 1,424 yards before being drafted by the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and embarking on a seven-year NFL career.

![Image 53](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/08/83e5e6d9-horace_copeland.jpg)His stellar exploits as a part of Miami’s track and field may be less known, but they were plenty impressive too.

Copeland became Miami’s first track All-American when he posted a fifth-place finish in the long jump at the 1992 NCAA Outdoor Track and Field Championships. That same season, Copeland was named the Most Outstanding Performer at the Big East Outdoor Track and Field Championships after he won the 100-meter, the long jump and anchored the Hurricanes’ 4×100-meter relay team to a win.

Copeland’s set multiple school records during his time with the Hurricanes track team and his name and marks still appear in the school record book. His mark of 7.74m in the indoor long jump ranks third in school history behind only Isaiah Holmes’ 8.03m and Russell Robinson’s 7.75m. Copeland’s mark of 7.87m in the outdoor long jump stood as the school record for nearly 30 years before Robinson eclipsed it in 2021 with a 7.99m.

Copeland was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2001.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Mike Fiore (Baseball, 1985-88)

Mike Fiore’s four-year career at Miami was marked by plenty of success.

![Image 54](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/08/5c52e706-mike_fiore.jpg)As a freshman, the New Jersey native hit .330 with 46 RBI and 11 doubles, a performance that helped him earn Freshman All-America honors from Baseball America. That same season, he helped lead the Hurricanes to the College World Series and the national title.

A year leader, he earned a spot on the All-College World Series Team after the Hurricanes returned to Omaha. He was a consensus All-American as a senior and became the only player in Miami’s storied baseball history to win the Dick Howser Trophy when he brought the honor home in 1987.

He finished his Miami career hitting .360 and his name still fills the Miami record book, with Fiore holding the program record for career at bats (946), runs scored (258), total bases (506), hits (341), walks (222), and RBI (235). His No. 12 jersey was retired, and Fiore was inducted into both the College Baseball Hall of Fame (2014) and the UM Sports Hall of Fame (2000).

After his time in Coral Gables, Fiore went on to win a gold medal with Team USA in the 1988 Seoul Olympic Games and after his retirement as a player, he worked for USA Baseball, eventually becoming a general manager for the organization. He is currently a vice president at the Boras Corporation.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Jenny Keim-Johansen (Women's Diving, 1997-2000)

Fort Lauderdale native Jenny Keim-Johansen added to Miami’s storied diving history during her time as a Hurricane.

![Image 57](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/08/c0f3e99d-jenny_keim.jpg)Keim-Johansen won two NCAA titles, earned six All-American honors and was named the Big East Diver of the Year in both 1999 and 2000. In 1999, she was also named the NCAA Diver of the Year.

She earned three All-American nods on both the 3-meter and 1-meter springboards and won the 1999 national championship on the 3-meter. A year later, she brought home the national title on the 10-meter platform. Keim-Johansen was also a five-time Big East champion and a two-time Olympian, representing Team USA at both the 1996 Summer Olympics in Atlanta and the 2000 Summer Games in Sydney.

After her career, she served as the head coach at both N.C. State and North Carolina and she and her husband, Drew, founded the American School for Diving in 2007.

Keim-Johansen was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2010.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Sean Taylor (Football, 2001-03)

Sean Taylor was a homegrown Hurricane whose legacy still resonates in South Florida, in Washington, D.C. and within the Hurricanes football program and Miami community.

![Image 58](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2020/06/5c19f69d-taylor_jones_fsu-1-400x400.jpg)

A three-sport star at Miami’s Gulliver Prep, Taylor arrived at Miami as a state champion in both football and track and field and it didn’t take long for him to get on the field and make an impact for the Hurricanes.

In 2001, he was one of just four true freshmen to see significant playing time on special teams during Miami’s run to the national championship. A year later, he stepped into the starting role vacated by two-time consensus All-American Ed Reed. That season, Taylor notched 87 tackles and had four interceptions, numbers that helped him earn first-team All-Big East recognition.

His numbers would only improve in 2003, when he hauled in 10 interceptions, three of which he returned for touchdowns. Taylor finished his junior season with 77 tackles and went on to earn recognition as a consensus All-American and the Big East Player of the Year.

Taylor had 14 career interceptions at The U, a number that still ranks fifth in program history and his 10 INTs in 2003 are tied for most in a single season with the 10 Bennie Blades collected in 1986.

In 2004, Taylor was one of a record six Hurricanes to hear their names called during the first round of the NFL Draft. Taylor was selected fifth overall by Washington and he played there for four seasons where he quickly earned a reputation as one of the fiercest hitters in the league. He was a 2006 Pro Bowl selection and was leading the NFL in interceptions with five when he died in November 2007.

After his death, Taylor was posthumously voted to the 2007 Pro Bowl and in 2008, was enshrined in Washington’s Ring of Honor. He was inducted into UM’s Ring of Honor in 2017 and into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2015.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Jodi Applebaum-Steinbauer (Women's Tennis, 1975-78)

A four-time All-American during her time at Miami, Jodi Appelbaum-Steinbauer made an impact not just on the Hurricanes’ tennis program, but on South Florida tennis as a whole.

![Image 61](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/08/ca9e1eb1-jodi_applebaum.jpg)Appelbaum-Steinbauer came to Coral Gables after a standout high school career at Miami Beach High, where she won a pair of state titles. Her success continued at the collegiate level where in 1977, she and partner Terry Salganik won the USTA doubles national title. That same year, she was a semifinalist in the singles competition.

A year later, Appelbaum-Steinbauer reached the USTA doubles finals for a second straight year, this time with partner Kim Sands. They finished as runners-up.

In Appelbaum-Steinbauer’s four years at Miami, the Hurricanes posted a 69-7 record and won the 1976 state championship. She won a bronze medal in singles and a silver medal in doubles for the U.S. in the 1977 Maccabiah Games and appeared in the 1981 U.S. Open.

Once her playing career ended, Appelbaum-Steinbauer served as the Tennis Director for the Junior Orange Bowl Committee for more than 25 years. During that time, Andy Murray, Coco Gauff, Andy Roddick, Francis Tiafoe, and Madison Keys – among others – all competed in the event as juniors.

Appelbaum-Steinbauer was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 1993 and served as the organization’s president from 2007-2009.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Jon Jay (Baseball, 2004-06)

Jon Jay grew up in Miami, attended Ron Fraser’s youth baseball camps at Mark Light Field, and helped lead Christopher Columbus High School to a state championship in 2003.

![Image 64](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2022/12/d1f4171e-30jay0528-003-400x400.jpg)

So, when it came time to play college baseball, there was little surprise Jay chose his hometown program – and the Hurricanes are certainly glad he did.

Jay had one of the most memorable freshman seasons in program history, hitting .368 with 56 RBI, six home runs, and 14 RBI. His batting average ranked third on the team, his RBI total was second and Jay was named a first-team Freshman All-American by both Baseball America and Collegiate Baseball. He helped lead the Hurricanes to the College World Series, where he earned a spot on the All-Tournament team after going 6 for 14 in Omaha with a triple, a home run and seven RBI.

There was no sophomore slump a year later, with Jay earning All-ACC honors after leading Miami with a .408 batting average. He also had 17 doubles, a home run and had 52 RBI. A year later in 2006, he once again led Hurricanes’ hitters, this time with a .361 average and a .490 on-base percentage. He also scored 77 runs, stole 31 bases and was a first-team All-ACC selection and second-team All-American.

Selected by the St. Louis Cardinals in the second round of the 2006 MLB draft, Jay had an 11-year professional career that included a World Series championship with the Cardinals and time with the San Diego Padres, Chicago Cubs, Kansas City Royals, Arizona Diamondbacks, Chicago White Sox, and the Los Angeles Angels.

In 2023, Jay joined the Miami Marlins coaching staff and today, he’s an assistant coach with the organization that drafted him, the Cardinals.

Jay was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2016.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

George Mira, Jr. (Football, 1960-62)

During his time at Miami, George Mira, Sr. set nearly every Hurricanes passing record.

![Image 65](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/08/1b7c4781-george_mira.jpg)The Key West native totaled 5,125 yards of offense, helped lead the Hurricanes to the 1961 Liberty Bowl – the program’s first bowl appearance in 19 years. A year later, he led the Hurricanes to the Gotham Bowl in New York City, where he threw for 348 yards despite playing in a snowstorm. The signal caller earned the nickname “The Matador” for his ability to both drop back and pass, and scramble when needed. He finished fifth in balloting for the Heisman Trophy in 1962 and was a first-team All-American that season.

He was selected by the San Francisco 49ers with the 15 th overall pick in the 1964 NFL Draft and played for 49ers, Philadelphia Eagles, Baltimore Colts and Miami Dolphins during an eight-year NFL career. He also played in both the Canadian Football League and the World Football League.

His No. 10 jersey is retired at Miami, and he was inducted into both the Miami Ring of Honor (1997) and the UM Sports Hall of Fame (1973).

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Art Saey (Boxing, 1944-47)

During his two years as a Hurricane, Art Saey went undefeated – and won most of his bouts via knockout. There was one stretch during his collegiate career in which he won 17 straight matches by knockout.

Robin Harmony (Women's Basketball, 1980-84)

Robin Harmony’s impact at Miami extended far beyond her playing days.

![Image 71](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/08/5e615fbe-robin_harmony.jpg)A native of Hershey, Pennsylvania, Harmony finished her Hurricanes career with 1,308 points, 760 rebounds, 445 assists and 314 steals. She returned to her alma mater as an assistant coach in 1985 and spent 17 seasons helping the Hurricanes women’s basketball team flourish under former head coach Ferne Labati.

Joaquin Gonzalez (Football, 1997-2001)

During his time at Miami’s Christopher Columbus High School, Joaquin Gonzalez was a force, playing both offensive and defensive line for the Explorers’ football team and competing on the school’s track team.

![Image 72](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2020/11/fa2e61f7-scan-091028-0063-400x400.jpg)

He’d eventually find ways to impact his hometown college football team, too.

After redshirting in 1997, Gonzalez earned Miami’s starting right tackle job as a redshirt freshman and went on to earn BIG EAST Rookie of the Year honors. He was the first offensive lineman to win the award.

He went on to earn All-American honors in 2000 and 2001 from the Football Writers Association of America and along with teammate Bryant McKinnie, anchored the Hurricanes’ offensive line during Miami’s 2001 national championship season. A four-year starter, he set a then-school record when he made his 49 th straight start in the Rose Bowl against Nebraska. He was also a four-time Big East All-Academic team member and received UM’s highest honor when he was inducted into Iron Arrow.

Gonzalez, who helped the Hurricanes average 454.8 yards and 43.2 points per game in 2001, was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2016.

Yolanda McCray (Women's Track & Field, 1996-99)

A four-time state champion at Miami Southridge High, Yolanda McCray brought a stellar resume with her to Coral Gables.

![Image 75](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/08/cb9a6317-yolanda_mccray.jpg)By the time she left Miami, that stellar resume was only longer.

McCray earned All-American honors six times during her Hurricanes career and in 1999, capped her stellar run at Miami by winning the national title in the 100-meter hurdles at the NCAA Outdoor Track & Field Championships.

Before winning that title, though, McCray won the 1997 Big East championships in the outdoor 100-meters, the outdoor 100-meter hurdles and the indoor 55-meter hurdles. That season, she was also named the Big East Outdoor Most Outstanding Track Athlete.

She also became only the second woman in conference history to win a second Big East Outdoor Most Outstanding Track Athlete award.

McCray, who was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2011, still holds some of the best times in program history. Her 7.54 in the 55-meter hurdles ranks second at Miami behind only Gillian Russell and her 8.04 in the 60-meter hurdles ranks third.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Rio Ramirez (Men's Diving, 1996-99)

More than two decades after his own days as a competitive diver at Miami, Rio Ramirez is still making a difference for the Hurricanes.

![Image 76](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2024/12/0aca1bb2-rio_ramirez-400x400.jpg)A former four-time national champion, Ramirez is in his second year as an assistant coach for the Hurricanes and already under his tutelage, Miami has added to its rich championship history with diver Chiara Pellacani winning the 1-meter national title last season.

In Ramirez, Pellacani and the Hurricanes know they have a championship-caliber mentor.

Ramirez won three straight NCAA 1-meter titles from 1997-1999 and the NCAA platform title in 1999. He was a five-time All-American and was twice named the NCAA Diver of the Year. He also won six Big East conference titles as a Hurricane.

His journey to Miami came with its share of twists and turns.

Before defecting to the United States, Ramirez was the Cuban national champion in both the 3-meter springboard and the platform and at age 16 in 1991, he won 10-meter gold medal at the Pan American Games.

He defected while competing in Puerto Rico in 1993 and three years later, enrolled at Miami where he’d not only go on to have a successful diving career, but earn a degree in business administration. He graduated from Miami in 2001 and was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2014.

Ramirez started his coaching career at FIU, where he led the Panthers to five straight conference titles and was named the Sun Belt Conference Coach of the Year in 2013 and the Conference USA Coach of the Year in 2014. He also coached at Alabama and Virginia Tech before returning to his alma mater.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Nathaniel Crosby (Men's Golf, 1979-82)

Nathaniel Crosby – the son of Bing Crosby – learned to play golf in part to spend time with his famous father, a longtime fan of the game.

![Image 79](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/08/67a4b748-nat_crosby.jpg)He wound up becoming an All-American at Miami.

Crosby, who was born and raised in California, joined the Hurricanes in 1979 and during the fall semester of his junior year, won the United States Amateur, one of the most well-known amateur golf tournaments in the world. He was 19 years and 10 months old at the time and became the third-youngest player to win that event. He won after a sudden-death playoff.

Crosby went on to earn recognition as the Florida Sports Writers Amateur Athlete of the Year and was also named North California’s Athlete of the Year. As a result of his win at the U.S. Amateur, Crosby was invited to play in the Masters Tournament in Augusta, the U.S. Open and several other major tournaments.

Crosby was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2005.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Doris Hart (Women's Tennis, 1947-49)

Doris Hart was born in St. Louis, grew up in Coral Gables and became not just a Miami tennis legend, but one of the game’s most decorated players.

![Image 82](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/08/020d61de-doris_hart.jpg)Hart reached 67 Grand Slam finals and won 35 titles, with her first – the 1947 Wimbledon doubles title – coming while she was still a student at Miami.

She’d go on to win the 1951 Wimbledon singles, doubles and mixed doubles titles; the 1954 U.S. National Ladies singles, doubles, and mixed doubles titles, and the 1955 U.S. National Ladies singles, doubles and mixed doubles titles as well. She also won the French Open twice and the Australian Open. She totaled 29 major doubles titles and was ranked No. 1 in the world in 1951. In all, she spent a decade ranked in the top 10.

Hart was inducted into the International Tennis Hall of Fame in 1969 and was a part of the UM Sports Hall of Fame’s inaugural induction class in 1967.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Jack McClinton (Men's Basketball, 2006-09)

Jack McClinton came to Miami as a transfer from Siena College in New York and had to wait his turn to suit up as a Hurricane.

![Image 83: Jack McClinton covers Devin Ginty.](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2014/10/87820188-middle_tixxdkvfcrzicnr.20120727153338-400x400.jpeg)

Once he was cleared to get on the court, though, McClinton made his time at Miami count.

He was a first-team All-ACC selection in both 2008 and 2009 and was a third-team selection in 2007. He scored 38 points in an NCAA Tournament game against St. Mary’s, and his name still appears all throughout the Miami record book.

He connected on 101 3-point field goals during the 2008-2009 season, a number that’s still the most by any Hurricane in a single season and his 1,702 career points still rank eighth all-time in school history.

McClinton was selected by the San Antonio Spurs in the second round of the 2009 NBA Draft and went on to play professionally in Israel, Turkey and Ukraine before retiring. His No. 33 jersey was honored by the basketball program and hangs in the rafters at the Watsco Center.

McClinton was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2022.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Wendy Williams (Women's Diving, 1985-89)

Wendy Williams grew up in a diving family and was one of the nation’s top high school diving recruits.

![Image 86](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/08/ccd0c8a6-wendy_williams.jpg)Needless to say, it was no surprise that the three-time high school All-American wasted little time making her presence felt once she joined the Hurricanes program.

Williams earned a second-place finish on the 3-meter springboard at her first NCAA Championships as a freshman. By the time she left Miami, she was a three-time All-American, a five-time U.S. national champion and a seven-time NCAA finalist. In 1989, she won the 10-meter NCAA platform title and finished third in both the 1-meter and 3-meter springboard events. Her performance that season – and at the NCAA championship meet – helped her earn recognition as the 1989 NCAA Diver of the Year.

Her success continued on the international stage.

Williams won the bronze on the platform at the 1988 Summer Olympics in Seoul, South Korea and a year later, won the 1989 World Cup Championship. She added another platform bronze at the 1991 World Championships.

After her diving career was over, Williams – who earned a degree in psychology from Miami – served as the national spokesperson for the Motions in Mind Depression Awareness Campaign sponsored by the Women’s Sports Foundation.

She was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2008.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Davian Clarke (Men's Track & Field, 1995-98)

Davian Clarke, a native of Jamaica, wasted little time making an impact on the men’s track program when he arrived at Miami.

![Image 89](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/07/8c74b4d3-davian_clarke.jpg)A state champion in the 400-meters at Piper High School in Sunrise, Clarke earned All-American honors as a freshman in his signature event and set a then-school record time of 45.22 when competing at Jamaican nationals.

His success only grew through the rest of his Miami career.

Clarke won his first national title as a Hurricane when he posted a time of 45.29 in the 400 at the NCAA outdoor championships in 1996. That summer, he competed with the Jamaican national team at the Summer Olympics in Atlanta and won a bronze medal as the anchor of the 4x400m relay team.

He won his second national title as a Hurricane at the 1998 NCAA indoor championships when he posted a time of 45.86 in the 400. That time stood as a school record until March of this year, when current Hurricane sprinter Solomon Strader posted a time of 45.74.

Clark still holds the school’s outdoor 200 and 400m records and won eight medals while competing internationally for Jamaica. He was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2009.

Santana Moss (Football, 1997-2000)

Throughout his Hurricanes career, Santana Moss found ways to use his explosive speed and dazzling athleticism to not only make big plays for the Miami football team, but to win medals for the Miami men’s track and field team, too.

![Image 90](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2020/09/2ff0cd0e-06moss0003-400x400.jpg)

The receiver, a Miami native who won a pair of track and field titles while at Carol City High School, was a second-team All-Big East selection in1998. A year later, he was a first-team selection and in 2000, Moss became the first player in league history to earn recognition as both the Big East Offensive Player of the Year and the Big East Special Teams Player of the Year. He was a first-team All-American, and his name still fills the Miami record book.

Moss finished his career with 2,546 receiving yards – the most in school history until last fall, when Xavier Restrepo became the program’s all-time leading receiver. His 4,394 career all-purpose yards are second in program history behind only Duke Johnson, and his 29 career touchdowns still rank seventh among all Hurricanes.

As a member of Miami’s track and field team, Moss earned recognition as the Big East Most Outstanding Field Performer when he won the conference championships in both the long jump and triple jump and like in football.

He was drafted by the New York Jets in the first round of the 2001 NFL Draft and spent four seasons in New York before being traded to Washington. With Washington, he earned a Pro Bowl nod and was a second-team All-Pro selection. Moss finished his NFL career with 732 catches for 10,283 yards and 66 touchdowns. He also had 1,451 return yards with three touchdowns.

Moss was named one of the 90 Greatest Washington Commanders as part of the team’s 90 th anniversary celebration and was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2011.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Chiara Pellacani (Women's Diving, 2024-present)

Chiara Pellacani hasn’t been a Hurricane all that long, but she’s already added her name to Miami’s storied diving history.

![Image 93](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/03/a06eeb4a-chiara_ncaa_podium-400x400.jpg)The redshirt junior from Italy did not compete for the Hurricanes her first year on campus in order to prepare for the 2024 Summer Olympics. After earning a fourth-place finish in Paris last summer, Pellacani made her Miami debut and made it count.

In March, she won the NCAA championship on the 1-meter springboard with a score of 354.65. She was the national runner-up in the 3-meter, an event she won at the ACC Championships a month earlier.

Pellacani was named the ACC Women’s Diver of the Year, the CSCAA Diver of the Year and was one of four finalists for the Class of 2025 Honda Sport Award for Swimming & Diving.

She is already a two-time All-American and has set her sights on winning both springboard titles next season.

“After we were done at NCAA’s, the first thing I told [head diving coach Dario di Fazio] is that next year, we’re going to win both,” Pellacani said. “So, that’s going to be the goal. But at the same time, I just want to enjoy the process, just like this season.”

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

David Wilkie (Men's Swimming, 1973-76)

One of the most decorated swimmers in Miami history, David Wilkie was a 13-time All-American, a three-time national champion and an Olympic gold medalist.

![Image 94](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2021/04/7d0db325-david-wilkie.jpeg)Wilkie, who hailed from Aberdeen, Scotland, won the NCAA title in the 200-yard breaststroke in 1973. He followed that with the NCAA title in the 100-yard breaststroke in 1974 and another title in the 200-yard breaststroke in 1976.

Also in 1976, he won gold in the 200m breaststroke at the Summer Olympics in Montreal with a world-record time of 2:15.11. His record stood for six years. Wilkie was named the European Swimmer of the Year three times and was named the Sportsman of the Year in England in 1976.

Wilkie was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 1987.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Andrew Burrow (Men's Tennis, 1984-87)

Andrew Burrow grew up playing tennis in his native South Africa, but that didn’t stop some of the biggest college programs in the United States from recruiting him. Ultimately, though, it was Miami where Burrow opted to play and at Miami where he was a force.

![Image 97](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/07/efdd5843-andrew_burrow.jpg)Burrow notched more than 100 wins and captured the NCAA men’s singles title in 1987 in a three-set match that saw him rebound after dropping the first set to Michigan’s Dan Goldberg.

“To win the tournament was very surreal. It was a huge accomplishment for me. I wasn’t expected to win. It was also great to win for The U,” Burrow said in 2012. “It was a great honor for me to be one of only a handful of UM players to ever win the singles title.”

The Hurricanes advanced to the NCAA Tournament in each of his four years in orange and green and once his time in Coral Gables came to an end, Burrow played professionally for three years.

Burrow was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2005.

Dawn Frady (Women's Swimming, 1973-76)

Miami’s women’s swimming team was a powerhouse during the 1970s and Dawn Frady was a big reason why.

![Image 100](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/07/be5a67f3-dawn_frady.jpg)In 1975, Frady won a pair of individual national titles in the 200 and 400-yard freestyle, pacing the Hurricanes and helping them win a team title that same year. She was also a part of Miami’s 1976 championship team.

Frady was a seven-time All-American during her career, earning that distinction in several events including the 100, 200, 400, and 1650-yard freestyle; the 200 and 400-yard freestyle relays; and the 400-yard medley relay. She left the program as the school record holder in the 100, 200 and 400-yard freestyle and her top time of 53.82 in the 100-yard free ranked among the top 25 times in the world.

Russell Maryland (Football, 1988-90)

Miami has won five national titles and produced dozens of NFL stars.

![Image 101](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/07/ae14f9ca-maryland_thumb-400x390.jpg)But only three times has a Hurricane heard his name called first in the NFL Draft.

Russell Maryland is one of those Hurricanes.

The Chicago native came to Miami and was a part of two national championship teams.

The defensive lineman totaled 279 tackles, 25 tackles for loss, and 20.5 sacks during his Hurricanes career. He was a consensus All-American in 1990, was UPI’s College Football Lineman of the Year that season and became the first Hurricane to win the Outland Trophy as the nation’s top interior lineman.

His success was not limited to the field and Maryland received Miami’s highest honor when he was inducted into Iron Arrow before his graduation. The Dallas Cowboys selected him with the top pick in the 1991 NFL Draft.

During his 10-year NFL career, he notched 375 tackles, 24.5 sacks, forced nine fumbles, had an interception, and scored once. He was a three-time Super Bowl champion, a 1993 Pro Bowl selection and was on the 1991 PFWA All-Rookie Team.

Maryland was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 2011 and the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2001.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Ronni Reis-Bernstein (Women's Tennis, 1985-88)

At Miami’s Sunset High, Ronni Reis-Bernstein won the state championship.

![Image 104](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/07/ae4a7b5e-ronnie_reis.jpg)She’d go on to have plenty of success at the college level – and beyond.

At Miami, Bernstein earned ITA All-American honors in both singles and doubles four times. She was named the NCAA Senior Player of the Year in 1998 after reaching the finals in doubles and semis in singles at the NCAA Tournament. As a sophomore, she and teammate Lise Gregory posted a 29-0 record and won both the NCAA doubles title and the ITA National Intercollegiate Indoor title. Bernstein posted a 103-21 mark in singles play during her Miami career and an 89-11 mark in doubles. The Hurricanes went 85-23 during her career and were the runners-up at the NCAA Championship in 1985.

Bernstein was a three-time member of the _Tennis Magazine_ Collegiate All-Star Team and was selected to the USTA Federation Cup team in 1986, 87, and 88.

After her Miami career ended, Bernstein played on the WTA Tour for two years, reaching a career-high world ranking of No. 30 in doubles and No. 78 in singles in 1989. She was also named the Rookie of the Year in 1989.

In 1997, Bernstein took over as coach at FIU, where she led the Panthers to five NCAA Tournament berths in 10 years. She is currently getting ready to start her 19 th season as head coach at Michigan, where she has led the Wolverines to 12 Big Ten championships, six Big Ten tournament titles, 12 NCAA Sweet 16 appearances, and the program’s first Final Four this past year.

Bernstein was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2000.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Sharon Berg (Women's Swimming, 1973-76)

There is no doubt Sharon Berg was a history-making pioneer at the University of Miami.

![Image 107](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/07/149450b3-sharon_berg.jpg)Berg, who began swimming when she was just 4-years-old and trained with former U.S. Olympic coach George Haines and nine-time Olympic medalist Mark Spitz, was one of the first four women to receive a swimming scholarship to attend Miami.

During her Hurricanes career, Berg was a four-time All-American and eventually became the first woman swimmer at The U to win individual national championships, bringing home the 1974 titles in both the 200-yard breaststroke and the 400-yard freestyle. Ted Hendricks (Football, 1966-68)

Nicknamed “the Mad Stork,” Ted Hendricks was a force on and off the football field.

![Image 108](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2023/05/bd3875c1-hendricks_roh-400x400.jpg)A three-sport star at Hialeah High School, Hendricks received both athletic and academic scholarship offers to attend Miami. He opted to accept the academic scholarship and as an honors student, majored in math and minored in psychology.

During his three seasons in orange and green, the defensive end totaled 327 tackles and was a two-time unanimous All-American.

In 1968, he was named the UPI Lineman of the Year and was fifth in Heisman Trophy voting, despite playing on the defensive side of the ball.

The Baltimore Colts made him a second-round pick in the 1969 NFL/AFL Draft and Hendricks went on to become one of the league’s most decorated linebackers.

He was a four-time Super Bowl champion, a four-time First-Team All-Pro selection, an eight-time Pro Bowler and was on both the NFL 75 th Anniversary All-Time Team and the NFL 100 th Anniversary All-Time Team. During his 15-year NFL career, he amassed 61 sacks, 26 interceptions, recovered 16 fumbles, scored four touchdowns and notched four safeties.

Hendricks was inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 1990, the College Football Hall of Fame in 1987 and the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 1980. His No. 89 jersey was retired by Miami in 1997.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Tim James (Men's Basketball, 1996-99)

Tim James was a homegrown Hurricane whose efforts helped reshape Miami basketball.

![Image 111: Men's Basketball All-American, 1999](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2018/02/e7e3497b-tim_james-400x400.jpg)He was a star at Miami Northwestern where he earned All-State recognition in both basketball and track. He finished his high school career as the Bulls’ all-time leader in points, rebounds, and blocked shots – while also setting a state record in the high jump with a mark of 7-feet, 2-inches.

Once he brought his skill and athleticism to Coral Gables, he helped the Hurricanes post four consecutive winning seasons and earn three straight postseason bids.

James was named to the Big East All-Rookie Team as a freshman, was a second-team All-Big East selection as a sophomore and was a first-team All-Big East selection his final two seasons at Miami. And while he was named the Co-Big East Player of the Year in 1999, his athletic success wasn’t limited to the hardwood. James also competed for Miami’s track and field team and won the Big East high jump title twice.

He was selected by the Miami Heat in the first round of the 1999 NBA Draft and spent time with the Heat, Charlotte Hornets and Philadelphia 76ers before playing overseas. His name can still be found all throughout the Miami record and his 1,713 career points still rank seventh in program history.

In 2008, James enlisted in the U.S. Army and after going through basic training, the Miami native was deployed to Iraq. He is believed to be the first former NBA player to enlist and serve in Iraq. His No. 40 jersey is one of two Miami men’s basketball jerseys to be retired and James was inducted into the UM Sports Hall of Fame in 2009.

_– Christy Cabrera Chirinos_

Kim Sands (Women's Tennis, 1974-78)

Kim Sands’ impact at Miami didn’t just come during her time as a student-athlete – and she did more than just play tennis for the Hurricanes.

![Image 112](https://storage.googleapis.com/miamihurricanes-com-prod/2025/07/85f3f3d0-kim_sands-300x400.jpg)The first Black female student-athlete to receive a scholarship to attend Miami, Sands played one season of basketball and four seasons of tennis at The U. During her time at Miami, she amassed an 82-13 record in singles play, a mark that still ranks 24 th in program history.

After her Miami career, she embarked on a 10-year professional career where she rose as high as No. 44 in the WTA singles rankings and No. 31 in the doubles rankings. She advanced to the second round of Wimbledon twice and the second round of the French Open three times.

She returned to her alma mater in 1990 to coach the women’s tennis team and in her eight seasons, the Hurricanes posted a 102-76 record with five Big East titles and five NCAA Tournament appearances. Abstract 

With digitization, social media has grown into an important channel among marketers because of its reach and effectiveness. Companies utilizing social media influencers in their marketing strategies, which enable them to do paid collaborations and thereby reveal about their products and services. With the help of social media influencers, it is possible to engage consumers to products, because consumers like the real content they produce, and find it reliable. Alongside with social media influencers, athletes can also do influencer marketing during their own career. 

The study was implemented in cooperation with the Finnish Olympic Committee, and its purpose was to find out how top athletes can use influencer marketing as part of sports sponsorship on Instagram. In the study was used qualitative research as a research method, and research data was collected through semi-structured interviews. The research was carried out by interviewing eight top athletes in the active phase of their careers, who are actively doing paid collaborations on social media. In order to improve the reliability of the research results, two sports managers were also interviewed for the research. 

The research showed that influencer marketing done in cooperation with companies helps athletes build their own personal brand after finding a common values, and this can help them with future employment after their sports career. Social media collaborations were also maintained an important sources of income. The number of social media followers and the athlete ’s success in their own career also have a strong influence on getting influencer marketing collaborations. Athletes should take advantage of the possibilities of social media as part of their own profession, either by themselves or with the help of others.

# 1.1 Research motivation 

Digitization and the internet have brought new ways to influence and marketing online. Web 1.0 enabled one-way sharing of information to consumers, while Web 2.0 allowed for adding content and establishing a connection. With this, for example, bloggers were able to display advertisements on their blog use content marketing. Web 3.0 introduced apps and mobile devices that accelerated the popularity of social media platforms such as Instagram and Facebook, allowing anyone to build an online followership. (Leung, Gu & Palmatier, 2022.) Marketers are increasingly using social media platforms to market products to consumers, as social media has an estimated 3.6 billion active users who spend more than 130 minutes on social media every day (Koay, Cheung, Soh & Teoh, 2022). During the COVID-19 pandemic, the role of digital marketing was further emphasized when sports fans were engaged in stakeholder groups and sports events were marketed. Fans were able to connect with each other by discussing and sharing information through various social media platforms. (Byon & Phua, 2021.) Companies utilize social media influencers (SMIs) to promote product-related information across multiple platforms (Koay et al., 2022). In 2020, influencer marketing represented a $10 billion industry, which is why only few companies launch marketing campaigns without collaborating on popular social media platforms such as Instagram or TikTok (Haenlein, Anadol, Farnsworth, Hugo, Hunichen & Welte, 2020). 

Social media influencers are people who use social media channels and have an established followership that follows the influencer regularly, finding their content interesting and reliable. 2.4.1 Rule 40 

The Olympics are known all over the world, and therefore a big event also attracts actors who want to benefit from the reputation of the Olympics without their right (Finnish Olympic Committee, 2018). Rule 40 was developed to 18 

regulate the trademark rights of the Olympic Games as well as the obligations and rights of the persons participating in the honors competitions. These are related to the fact that their names, voices, images, personalities, or performances may not be used for commercial purposes during the Olympics. However, the rule covers all commercial activities that can be carried out in various communication channels. These communication channels include outdoor advertising, television, print, digital media, media advertising and social media. All persons who are accredited for the competition must follow Rule 40 throughout the competition. (Olympic Team Finland, 2020.) The Rule 40 is based on the fact that athletes are given permission to focus on sports during prestigious competitions, and commercial exploitation is handled by the people who have the right to do so (Finnish Olympic Committee, 2018). Persons accredited to the Olympic Games must follow the given instructions regarding communication and marketing. Athletes have been given the authority to thank their own partners once during the competition on a social media channel of their choice, but the thank you messages must not contain commercial or official logos of Olympic Games. Athletes can therefore produce content for their own social media channels within the limits allowed by the Finnish Olympic Committee and the International Olympic Committee. (Olympic Team Finland, 2018). 

2.4.2 Ambush marketing 

Ambush marketing refers to a practice where a competing company tries to steal the public ’s attention from the sponsoring company (Scott et al., 2021). A company that does not own the marketing rights to the event uses ambush marketing to create a connection. Its idea is to utilize the benefits of sponsorship without the sponsor ’s obligations (Nufer, 2016). The ambush company is not an official sponsor of the Olympics, but tries to associate itself indirectly with the event, in order to receive the benefits associated with an official sponsor. The ambush company can use phrases, images or symbols to make people believe that they are somehow related to the Olympics. A company engaged in ambush marketing can, for example, appear in the event ’s surroundings and thus divert attention away from the real sponsor of the event (Nufer, 2016). The 1996 Summer Olympics, where Nike, which was not an official sponsor of the Olympics, had a large waving logo on the building opposite the Olympic Stadium (Jones, 2018). Ambush marketing can also be seen as an activity where an unofficial sponsor takes advantage of awareness or attention without being the official sponsor of the event (Nufer, 2016). At the 2000 Summer Olympics in Sydney, many swimmers were seen in several photos wearing Adidas bodysuits. Because the swimming team received a lot of publicity during the Games, Adidas became the seventh most famous sports sponsor, even though Adidas was not an official sponsor of the Olympics. (Jones, 2018.) 19

time, money and energy can be considered personal resources. 3.2.2 Halo effect theory 

The halo effect theory is based on the fact that something that has a positive feature that attracts attention is also associated with other positive features. Consumers evaluate the product based on the review they receive from the product user. Brands use public figures to create a positive image of a certain product, to create a halo effect. (Djafarova & Rushworth, 2017.) When talking about the halo effect, it can be considered a kind of cognitive bias, on the basis of which people form positive or negative opinions about the properties of products 24 

towards another attribute. This means that the evaluation of some properties may have an effect on other properties. (Nicolau, Mellinas & Martín-Fuentes, 2020.) The halo effect works in two directions, whereby positive information produces positive thoughts and negative information leads to the evaluation of negative things. In marketing communications, public figures are used as help to create a halo effect. When a celebrity talks about a new product, the celebrity ’s good image is transferred to the advertised product, and through that, consumers get the impression that the advertised product is also believable. (Nufer, 2019.) Public figures are also used in advertising because of the halo effect, as it is easy to create a positive image with them. When a public figure everyone knows talks about a product, it creates an image in people ’s minds that the advertised product is also good, because the positive image of the public figure is transferred directly to the advertised product. (Yuan & Gao, 2022.) The halo effect can also be talked about in the context of sports. Fans can also show loyalty to the sponsors of the sports clubs they support through the halo effect, which leads to positive attitudes towards the sponsor ’s brand. (Nufer, 2019.) As stated above, the halo effect can not only have a positive effect, but also a negative one. If the athlete loses the game, it can also have a negative effect on the reliability or competence of the less well-known sponsoring company in the manner of a halo effect.  (Yuan & Gao, 2022.) 

3.2.3 WoM and eWoM 

Communication between customers is considered credible, which is why many customers would rely on the experiences of others in moments of uncertain choices. Consequently, WoM affects customer engagement, because it has an impact on what kind of attitudes customers develop, as well as how they behave. (Goyal & Verma, 2021.) Personal conversations shape consumer expectations, increase presuppositions and perceptions of after using a product or service (Jalilvand, Esfahani & Samiei, 2011). WoM can be considered more influential than regular media channels because positive WoM can lead to long-term customer relationships, while negative WoM can lead to more dissatisfied customers (Goyal & Verma, 2021). Consumers therefore share information and opinions with each other, and these shared issues lead buyers to products, brands and services, or alternatively away from them (Jalilvand et al., 2011). Traditional WoM, or word-of-mouth, has played a large role when looking at customers ’

purchase decisions (Hennig-Thurau, Gwinner, Walsh & Gremler, 2004). With the development and increased use of Web 2.0 technology, information has started to be shared more and more online, on the basis of which the new term eWoM or electronic word-of-mouth has been born (Wandoko & Panggati, 2022). 

EWoM is defined by Hennig-Thurau et al. (2004) in the article that it is any opinion made visible via the Internet to a number of people or companies, whether positive or negative, originating from a previous, current or potential customer, and related to a company or product. Communication related to eWoM can be carried out in discussion forums, newsgroups or web-based 25 

opinion platforms. (Hennig-Thurau et al., 2004.) Sharing opinions and information between companies and consumers is easy via Internet (Jalilvand et al., 2011). According to Wandoko & Panggati (2022), companies use digital influencers in their business to share product information through eWoM Wandoko & Panggati, 2022). According to Uzunoglu & Kip (2014), digital influencers ’ own experiences and opinions, which are shared using eWoM, can be considered more reliable than the company ’s own communication (Uzunoglu & Kip, 2014). Factors influencing positive eWoM in social media include self-expression, relationships with other users, and brand-related relationships (Choi, Thoeni & Kroff, 2018). It has also been found that social media influencers can create positive eWoM towards a brand (Choi et al., 2018; Khan, Zaman, Khan & Musleha, 2022). Passive users of social media have been transformed into active participants who communicate with their own networks and share images, videos or written texts. Since the sharing of one ’s thoughts on social media has grown recently, eWoM has an increasingly greater influence on consumers ’

purchasing decisions. (Leon, Loi & Woon, 2022.) EWoM is now considered as reliable as brands ’ own websites (Jalilvand et al., 2011).

The influencer creates and pub-lishes a product recommendation post on their own channel and receives a re-ward in return. When it is a paid commercial partnership, the author of the pub-lication must inform about it in connection with the post in order to avoid mis-leading. Consumers usually engage with social media posts for non-commercial reasons. Therefore, subtly announcing paid advertisements can irritate consum-ers and cause them to have negative feelings. This creates challenges for social media influencers, as their income may be completely dependent on collabora-tions with brands. Many influencers have said on their own social media chan-nels that they do paid collaborations so that it is possible for them to offer quality content to their followers, and so that they receive income. By collaborating with a social media influencer, companies want to increase their sales and increase a positive brand attitude. (Stubb et al. 2019.) Ibáñez-Sánchez et al. (2021) were men-tioned in the article, when an influencer cooperates with a brand that is well-known, more positive effects have been observed from the consumer ’s point of view. In this case, a well-known influencer and a well-known brand strengthen 28 

each other, making marketing through social media more effective. (Ibáñez-Sánchez et al., 2021.) 

According to Belanche et al., (2020), consumers can be divided into two groups when examining the effect of their participation in collaborative publica-tions. Involved consumers are more interested in learning about products and seek information to facilitate decision-making, while less involved consumers simplify their own selection process. Engaged consumers pay more attention to advertised messages and do not perceive commercial content as a negative thing. On the other hand, less engaged consumers do not pay as much attention to com-mercial messages and are not affected in the same way. Therefore, when there is a connection (fit) between the influencer and the consumer, the participation and interest of the followers increases. Active followers of influencers are more inter-ested in the products advertised in collaborations when the publications coincide. Consistent and regular content publishing by influencers causes positive activity in followers. Consequently, active followers believe in influencers and follow their advice also in paid collaborations. Followers who use products are more active in searching for information about advertised products and follow influ-encers ’ accounts on social media because they have a positive attitude towards paid collaborations. It is important that the company and the influencer cooper-ate strongly and create a story behind the advertised product. (Belanche et al., 2020.) 29
